Frequently Asked Questions

What is at stake in Zambia’s election on 13 August?

President Hakainde Hichilema is seeking a second five-year term on the strength of an economic recovery plan following the country’s 2020 sovereign default, facing Brian Mundubile of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity, standard-bearer of the Tonse-Pamodzi alliance backed by former ruling party structures. Zambia is one of the world’s top copper producers with 8.79 million registered voters, and while the government cites progress on debt restructuring, growth and inflation, the cost of living remains voters’ dominant concern.

What concerns have been raised about the campaign?

The Electoral Commission of Zambia has revoked an accreditation with immediate effect, a Zambian journalist has been detained under the Cyber Crimes Act over a leaked audio recording, and Brian Mundubile of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity has seen his running mate, Makebi Zulu, appear on stage in a bulletproof vest. Reporting has also cited alleged state interference, restrictions on opposition activity and contested legislative changes, against a national record of three peaceful transfers of power through the ballot box.

What did the African Development Bank approve for the Lobito Corridor?

On 6 August the Bank’s board approved a $255 million loan from the African Development Fund and a $10 million grant from the Rome Process and Mattei Plan Financing Facility for Zambia’s participation, funding roughly 550 kilometres of new railway inside Zambia and upgrading 105 kilometres of the Mwinilunga to Jimbe road. It is the first tranche under ADF-16, with later phases envisaged to reach around $500 million, and is expected to create some 500 permanent and 5,000 temporary jobs.

How severe is the Congolese Ebola outbreak?

More than 1,900 people have died, and between 60 and 70% of those deaths occur within communities before patients reach a treatment centre. That distribution points to distance, transport and trust in the health system rather than to the characteristics of the disease itself.

Sources: African Development Bank, allAfrica, Zambian Eye, Associated Press via Washington Post

World.title: From Security to Property maintenance: Service businesses Belizeans should consider!
World.content:
From Security to Property maintenance: Service businesses Belizeans should consider!

By Zoila Palma: When we talk about jobs and economic opportunities in Belize, the conversation often focuses on becoming a teacher, nurse, police officer, accountant or obtaining a university degree.

But there is another side of the economy that deserves far more attention: service-based businesses.

From tourism and transportation to security, technology, maintenance and skilled trades, Belize needs people who can provide reliable services to households, businesses and visitors.

The demand is being driven by the growth and changing needs of the economy.

Belize’s 2026 national budget reported that job creation in 2025 was driven by service-oriented industries, particularly wholesale and retail trade and tourism.

Tourism remains one of the country’s major economic engines, supporting tens of thousands of jobs directly and indirectly. The World Bank has also identified skilled-labour shortages in Belize and says its new country strategy will focus on developing a better-skilled workforce.

So, what types of service businesses could Belize use more of?

Tourism and Experience Services

Examples: tour companies, tour guides, transportation services, eco-tourism operators, cultural tours, fishing and adventure excursions, event planners and destination-management companies.

Tourism creates opportunities far beyond hotels and restaurants. The World Bank’s current Belize strategy identifies tourism as an important area for investment and job creation.

Security Services

Examples: private security companies, security guards, CCTV installation and monitoring, alarm systems, access-control systems and security consulting.

As businesses, homes, construction sites and commercial properties expand, there is an opportunity for professional security companies offering more than traditional guards. Belize is also investing heavily in security infrastructure, including communications systems and an AI-enabled systems, creating opportunities for people trained in security technology.

Cleaning and Property-Maintenance Services

Examples: residential cleaning, commercial cleaning, post-construction cleaning, landscaping, lawn care, pressure washing, pool maintenance and property caretaking.

This is an area where relatively small businesses can start with limited equipment and grow. Hotels, offices, rental properties, restaurants, schools and homeowners all require regular maintenance.

Construction and Home-Improvement Services

Examples: electrical work, plumbing, carpentry, welding, masonry, painting, roofing, cabinetry, tiling, air-conditioning installation and general maintenance.

These are exactly the kinds of practical skills that can become businesses. A trained electrician, plumber, carpenter or welder does not necessarily need to wait for someone to hire them—they can build a customer base and eventually employ other Belizeans.

Information Technology and Digital Services

Examples: computer repair, website development, cybersecurity, cloud services, data analysis, digital marketing, graphic design and IT support.

The Government of Belize has identified cybersecurity, data analysis, UI/UX design and cloud engineering as among the most in-demand and currently lacking skills in the country’s global digital services sector.

Transportation and Delivery Services

Examples: airport transfers, tourist transportation, courier services, delivery companies, moving services, refrigerated transportation and specialized freight services.

As tourism, e-commerce, construction and business activity grow, so does the need to move people and products efficiently. Transportation is also closely connected to tourism and other sectors, meaning a well-run transportation company can serve multiple markets.

Agricultural and Agro-Processing Services

Examples: farm services, irrigation installation, agricultural equipment repair, food processing, packaging, cold storage, transportation and agricultural consulting.

Agriculture is not only about farming. There are businesses to be created around the farmer—from planting and harvesting services to processing, packaging, storage and transportation.

But for Belizeans to take advantage of these opportunities, we must also invest in the skills needed to provide these services.

Belize therefore needs to promote technical and vocational education, apprenticeships and entrepreneurship at the same time.

Schools can expose students to trades and practical skills earlier, businesses can provide more apprenticeship opportunities, and training institutions can work closely with employers to identify the skills the economy actually needs.

The goal should not only be to prepare young Belizeans to look for jobs, but also to equip them with the skills to create businesses, provide needed services and, eventually, employ others.

World.title: The skills Belize needs most: Why we need to promote Vo-Tech
World.content:
The skills Belize needs most: Why we need to promote Vo-Tech

By Zoila Palma: There is a growing conversation in Belize about education, employment and the skills young people need to build successful careers.

While university degrees remain important for many professions, there is also a constant need for people with practical, technical and vocational skills.

The World Bank noted that shortages of skilled labour are evident in Belize and identified workforce skills development as a priority for the country’s economic growth.

Among the skills that deserve greater attention are construction and carpentry, electrical installation, plumbing, automotive and heavy-duty mechanics, welding and metal fabrication, refrigeration and air-conditioning, nursing and healthcare support, information technology and computer repair, hospitality and culinary skills, and agriculture and agro-processing.

These are not simply jobs that can be done while waiting for a “better” career.

They are essential services that homes, businesses, hotels, farms, factories and communities depend on every day.

Our TVET system already provides training pathways in trades at different levels, including programs designed to prepare students for entry-level and skilled work.

The need for these skills also creates opportunities for entrepreneurship.

A trained electrician can start an electrical business.

A welder can open a fabrication shop.

A mechanic can establish an auto-repair service.

A carpenter can build furniture, cabinets and homes.

A trained refrigeration technician can provide services to households, supermarkets, restaurants and hotels.

With the right training, tools, work ethic and business skills, a vocational qualification can become more than a job—it can become a source of income and employment for others.

This is why Belize needs to promote technical and vocational education and training, or TVET, much more aggressively.

For too long, young people have sometimes been given the impression that success means going to university and earning a traditional degree, while vocational careers are treated as a second option.

That mindset needs to change.

An ILO analysis published earlier this year specifically examined Belize’s TVET system and emphasized the importance of developing, recognizing and certifying skills while improving access to training and the labour market.

The question should not be whether a young person chooses university or vocational training.

The better question is: What skills does Belize need, and how can we prepare our young people to fill those gaps?

We need schools, parents, policymakers and businesses to expose students earlier to trades and technical careers, expand apprenticeships and hands-on training, and make vocational education something students can be proud of.

Belize does not only need more people with certificates and degrees—it needs people who can build, repair, install, create, care, cook, design, troubleshoot and produce.

If there is always a need for these skills, there should always be a strong effort to train Belizeans to fill thsse jobs.

World.title: International News: Solar Eclipse plunges parts of Europe into darkness in spectacular display
World.content:
International News: Solar Eclipse plunges parts of Europe into darkness in spectacular display

By Zoila Palma: Millions of people gathered across parts of Europe today to witness a rare total solar eclipse, with stunning images capturing the moment the Moon moved directly between the Earth and the Sun. Large crowds equipped with lawn chairs, umbrellas and hats gathered across northern and central Spain, while parts of Iceland and Greenland also had opportunities to observe the celestial event.

In Iceland, daylight briefly turned into darkness along the western coastline as the eclipse reached totality. Despite concerns about cloudy weather, skies cleared in some areas, allowing residents and tourists to witness the rare phenomenon. In Reykjavik, crowds reportedly cheered as the sky suddenly went dark near the iconic Hallgrímskirkja church. Totality was expected to last less than two and a half minutes, with the eclipse reaching its peak over the waters west of Iceland.

Spain was expected to attract as many as 6 million visitors to rural areas along the eclipse’s path and the Balearic Islands. Officials urged spectators to avoid areas affected by an ongoing heatwave because of increased wildfire risks. The event was particularly significant for Spain, where a total solar eclipse had not been visible across the Iberian Peninsula since 1912.

A total solar eclipse occurs when the Moon completely blocks the Sun’s light, temporarily darkening the day and creating dramatic changes in the sky and surrounding environment. Scientists are also using the event as an opportunity for research, with NASA planning to operate a high-altitude aircraft from Iceland to track the Moon’s shadow while balloon missions study changes in the lower atmosphere. Spain is scheduled to experience another total solar eclipse on August 2, 2027, followed by an annular eclipse in January 2028.

World.title: Climate Finance Unit, CABEI and partners discuss climate priorities
World.content:
Climate Finance Unit, CABEI and partners discuss climate priorities

By Zoila Palma: The Climate Finance Unit (CFU) convened a strategic meeting with the Central American Bank for Economic Integration (CABEI), Development Finance Corporation (DFC), and the Caribbean Community Climate Change Centre (CCCCC) this week to discuss regional and national initiatives and explore opportunities for collaboration.

Participants included Manfred Kopper, Chief Sustainability Officer, CABEI; Mansfield Blackwood, Assistant Executive Director, CCCCC; and Mario Lara, Chief Financial Officer, DFC, alongside the CFU team.

“As key partners in advancing Belize’s access to climate finance, the discussions provided an opportunity to strengthen coordination, identify areas for collaboration, and support the mobilization of resources for Belize’s climate and development priorities,” the unit explained.

The goal is to advance climate-resilient development for Belize.

World.title: International News: U.S. poll shows more than 80% of high school students used AI for homework
World.content:
International News: U.S. poll shows more than 80% of high school students used AI for homework

By Zoila Palma: An estimated 84% of U.S. high school students surveyed reported using generative artificial intelligence for schoolwork in 2025, highlighting the growing role of AI in education.

The figure, reported by the College Board, comes as educators grapple with concerns about students using chatbots to produce essays, reading responses, lab summaries and other assignments within seconds.

A survey conducted between spring 2025 and spring 2026 among 303 educators and school professionals in Wisconsin, along with 132 professionals from schools across the United States, found that academic dishonesty and plagiarism were among the leading concerns surrounding AI use.

About 65% of Wisconsin respondents identified those issues as a concern, compared with 74% of respondents in the broader national sample, Fortune reports.

Educators also expressed concern about whether traditional assignments can accurately measure what students understand when AI can generate polished responses.

Nearly half of Wisconsin respondents, 47%, said difficulty assessing student learning when AI is used was a concern, while the figure rose to 53% nationally.

The growing use of AI has also led some teachers to turn to AI-detection tools, but their reliability remains a concern.

A 2025 national survey found that 43% of sixth- through 12th-grade public school teachers regularly used AI-detection applications, while another 27% had experimented with them. However, research has found that these tools can produce significant false positives and false negatives, leading some educators to instead require students to demonstrate their work through in-class writing, oral explanations, handwritten assignments or other methods that provide clearer evidence of independent thinking.

World.title: Sea Cucumber fishing season opening soon
World.content:
Sea Cucumber fishing season opening soon

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Fisheries Department officially announced the opening of the 2026–2027 sea cucumber fishing season, pursuant to the Fisheries Resources (Sea Cucumber) Regulations under Statutory Instrument No. 107 of 2022.

The season will commence on September 1, 2026, and continue through January 31, 2027, or until the national catch quota is fully realized, whichever occurs first.

The public is advised that commercial fishing operations will be permitted in fishing areas 2 through 8 only; fishing area 1 will remain closed for the duration of the season.

Fishers holding a valid commercial fishing license who are interested in participating in the upcoming harvest must apply for a Special Sea Cucumber Fishing License in accordance with Statutory Instrument No. 67 of 2009.

Applications will be accepted during the period of August 18–31, 2026.

The special license fee is BZ$75.00.

All fishers on board any vessel engaged in sea cucumber fishing must possess a valid special sea cucumber fishing license.

The Fisheries Department urges all commercial fishers to complete their licensing applications early and strictly adhere to all guidelines to support the sustainability of the marine ecosystem.

World.title: Independent senators warn against telecom monopoly
World.content:
Independent senators warn against telecom monopoly

By Zoila Palma: The 4 Independent Senators have jointly raised strong objections to the proposed acquisition of Speednet Communications Limited (SMART) by Belize Telemedia Limited (BTL), stating that they were never consulted about the proposed transaction.

In a joint statement issued today, Senators Kevin Herrera, Glenfield Denison, Rev. Louis Wade and Janelle Chanona said they are seeking information from key authorities regarding the proposed acquisition.

The senators said no representative of BTL or any third party acting on the company’s behalf has contacted them or their respective organizations to discuss the acquisition.

They stated categorically that “No invitation from Belize Telemedia Limited (BTL), verbal or written, has ever been received by any of the Independent Senators or their respective organizations.”

As part of their efforts to obtain greater transparency, the Independent Senators said they have each signed and sent letters to the Chair of the Public Utilities Commission, the Attorney General, the Chairman of BTL’s Board and the Office of the Prime Minister.

The letters seek information they consider relevant to the proposed acquisition of Speednet Communications.

“The Independent Senators have signed and sent separate letters…to directly request information related and relevant to the proposed acquisition of Speednet Communications (SMART),” the statement said.

The senators also made clear their position on the potential impact of the transaction on Belize’s telecommunications sector.

They warned against concentrating the country’s telecommunications services under a single provider, stating, “We believe any decision to transform the telecommunications landscape into a monopoly is regressive.”

World.title: International Youth Day 2026 highlights skills, opportunities and shared aspirations
World.content:
International Youth Day 2026 highlights skills, opportunities and shared aspirations

By Zoila Palma: Nearly 1.3 billion people between the ages of 15 and 24 are living around the world, making today’s youth population the largest generation of young people to date. According to the United Nations, the demographic distribution of youth is expected to shift significantly, with 69 percent projected to live in low- and lower-middle-income countries by 2050, compared with 59 percent in 2025.

The UN also projects that the youth population in high- and upper-middle-income countries will decline by nearly 24 percent between 2025 and 2050. Meanwhile, injuries remain a major concern for young people, accounting for nearly half of all youth deaths in low-income countries and more than half of youth deaths in upper-middle- and high-income countries.

For International Youth Day 2026, the UN Youth Office is emphasizing the importance of future-ready skills as young people navigate a rapidly changing world.

These skills include digital and artificial intelligence literacy, as well as human-centered abilities such as critical thinking, empathy and resilience. The UN is also calling for more equitable access to skills development while recognizing young people as co-creators of education and policy, rather than simply recipients.

This year’s theme, “Different Contexts, Common Aspirations,” highlights the shared goals of young people despite differences in their communities and countries.

Young people continue to seek dignity, opportunity, meaningful participation, decent work, quality education and a sustainable future.

World.title: US$25-m yacht bet
World.content:
Jamaican American businessman Denton Douglas is confident that within three years a boatbuilding plant he is establishing in Jamaica will be an international success.Photo: Karl Mclarty

JAMAICAN American businessman Denton Douglas is embarking on an ambitious plan to take his boatbuilding business to Jamaica and is prepared to spend US$25 million, initially, to make it a success.

Douglas, who operates Monarch Yachts — a Florida-headquartered company which began operations in China and now operates two plants in Turkey — is pushing to open a yacht-building and repair facility in Jamaica and is confident that within three years it will become profitable while employing scores of Jamaicans.

“I want Jamaica to be a manufacturing hub. Over the years we have been mainly on primary goods; we export bananas, we export ore, but we never make something. We import our cars. We import everything else. I want to move Jamaica from that primary [producer] to a manufacturing hub, and I think we have the know-how. For sure we have the skills, and we have the logistics to do it,” Douglas told the Jamaica Observer on Sunday.

“We make luxury yachts, commercial boats like fishing boats. We also have ferries… for shuttling people… and our biggest business now are military boats, which is surprisingly patrol boats. We have a line of patrol boats and we have a contract for a country in Africa to do 20 to 40 small ferries… and about 10 patrol boats… We want to do that here because those are easy to build,” added Douglas, who wants to start operating locally before the end of this year.

The Munro College graduate, who received a track scholarship to study at Howard University in the United States in 1988, worked on Wall Street for years before moving into the boating business some 20 years ago.

“When I was in China we were price-competitive, [but] my idea was this: Anyone can come cheaper than you are; they can cut more corners and be cheaper. So I changed my business to quality, meaning… no one in the world can make a better yacht,” declared Denton, who now designs and builds yachts for some of the world’s super-rich.

He said Monarch’s services, which include yacht design, construction, brokerage, charters, and refits/repairs, can all be done in Jamaica, which would be convenient for many of the company’s clients.

“I want to come here and build yachts. Why? First, to be selfish. I fly 12 hours every time to Turkey and Italy to the shipyard, or 21 hours to China. An hour and a half [from Miami to Jamaica] is a lot better than flying so long,” said Douglas.

He pointed out that a customer in the US can jump on a plane in the morning, view his yacht in production in Jamaica and be back in the US the same day, something that cannot happen where he now operates in Turkey.

In addition, it will be much cheaper to build a yacht in Jamaica and ship it to the US.

“For example, my 45-footer, to take it from Turkey to the United States, it’s US$50,000. If I build that same boat here, I’m saving that much money. To take that boat from China is another US$25,000, so that’s US$75,000,” said Douglas as he pointed to the practicality of operating on the island.

According to Douglas, he is now in talks with local authorities to identify a site to set up shop, and while he would love it to be based in St Elizabeth, where he is from, for practical reasons the main shipyard will be in the eastern end of the island — either the Corporate Area, St Catherine, or Portland.

“We need access to skilled labour and access to a port. The key thing is an airport, so if an American businessman comes to Jamaica, comes to see his boat, [he can] fly in [to Jamaica in] the morning, see his yacht, and fly back. So we need somewhere that’s close to an airport where you have access to skilled labour,” said Douglas.

He added that, while his shop will be in one location, the operation could be islandwide as Monarch will operate differently from the American yacht companies which manufacture everything in a single plant.

“I want to adopt the European model, where the shipyard may be in Kingston, but the woodwork could be in St Elizabeth. The piping could be somewhere else, so the wealth and the labour skills are spread throughout Jamaica. So everyone benefits, not just one area,” declared Douglas.

He told the Observer that the plan is not just to build boats, but to establish an ecosystem that will include carpenters, welders, seamstresses, and others who will contribute to all aspects of the production of the yachts.

Douglas said he has already made contact with the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce and Jamaica Promotions Corporation (Jampro) which are helping with his application for a special economic zone (SEZ) designation, while Caribbean Maritime University (CMU) has already indicated its readiness to help with the training of workers.

“What I would do first is take a bunch of Jamaicans to China and Turkey and teach them on-the-job how it works. Then, once they get a basic understanding of whether it’s aluminium welding, steel welding for marine, or fibreglass, or epoxy work, then they will come back and start working.

“And so it will be maybe 15 to 20 foreign nationals and the rest Jamaicans. If it’s 100 Jamaicans, it will be 10 foreign nationals. It’s more of a teaching model, not a working model,” said Douglas.

“It’s just once we get the right people who can learn and are extremely meticulous, then we’ll be successful. The goal is never to have a lot of foreigners working at the shipyard. It’s always to have them teach us at the shipyard. That is the only way I’m going to do it. If I was going to have a lot of foreigners, I might as well stay where I am in Turkey,” Douglas explained.

He said Monarch will be prepared to pay the tuition for Jamaicans to study at CMU and work for the company for a period under a bonded arrangement.

“But I expect many of them to move on to companies in Germany and Italy because they will be able to pay them more. One of the highest-paid engineers on a yacht now is Jamaica[n],” said Douglas.

World.title: Rewarding resilience
World.content:
From left: Executive director at Sandals Foundation Heidi Clarke; consultant paediatrician at Falmouth Public General Hospital Dr Kerry-Ann McKenzie; Minister of Tourism Edmund Bartlett; and director of operations at Sandals Foundation Karen Zacca engage in conversation during Tuesday’s launch of Sandals Foundation’s Island Challenge Jamaica 2026 at AC Hotel Kingston. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

CONSULTANT paediatrician at Falmouth Public General Hospital Dr Kerry-Ann McKenzie was visibly moved, Tuesday, as she welcomed the Sandals Foundation’s annual Island Challenge, which will raise £100,000 to replace paediatric and neonatal equipment destroyed by Hurricane Melissa.

Operating out of Trelawny, a parish still recovering from last October’s devastation, McKenzie shared that even after the hospital replaced its roof, the paediatric unit’s Accident and Emergency Department looked forlorn, with only one bed to spare.

“We were pretty much very badly affected by Hurricane Melissa, and our paediatric unit was destroyed. We lost everything; every incubator, every monitor, every bed except one, our departments, where we fight every single day for the lives of our smallest, and our future leaders of our country were devastated,” said McKenzie, her voice trembling slightly.

She was extending her thanks to the Sandals Foundation during the launch of the annual Island Challenge at the AC Hotel Kingston.

Beginning October 2, the four-day expedition will take 30 athletes from the United Kingdom and 15 Jamaican participants across Trelawny, St Ann, St Mary, and St Andrew, where they will trek, hike, and paddle around the island to raise funds for paediatric equipment at Falmouth Public General Hospital.

McKenzie told the launch that doctors and nurses have been resilient in the face of disaster, showing up daily despite not having the equipment to provide comprehensive care. She noted that she was happily anticipating the addition of the medical instruments.

“Jamaicans are resilient. We are a resilient people, and we’re a resilient health facility. With the help of Sandals Foundation, we are going to show forth brighter than what we were previously.

“But resilience can’t buy an incubator. It can’t replace a cardiac monitor. It cannot give us back the beds that we lost. That’s why we’ve joined the Sandals Foundation now in this Island Challenge in getting us the essential equipment that we need for our paediatric and neonatal units at the Falmouth Public General Hospital,” she said.

Speaking with the Jamaica Observer, McKenzie explained that the paediatric unit was badly in need of beds, incubators, resuscitators, and monitoring equipment such as pulse oximeters, vital signs monitors, as well as phototherapy lights, warming blankets, and cooling blankets.

“We’ve struggled, but we have been able to keep the department afloat despite the lack of resources. We’re really looking forward to getting the extra help that we need to do what we need to do. We’ve had to do a lot of transfers out because we just don’t have the capacity to keep as many children as we want. But there are scenarios where we can’t get babies out and we’ve really had to take our hand and make fashion. It’s been an exhausting journey, but this is the beginning of a new one, so I’m so excited,” she said.

The head paediatrician also extended her gratitude to athletes participating in the event, telling the launch that their contribution to the hospital’s recovery was invaluable.

“To every runner, every hiker, every donor, every partner standing with us today, on behalf of every child that will pass through the doors of Falmouth Public General Hospital, and every family who will sit beside them holding their hands, we say thank you. You’re not just raising funds. You’re giving our children a lifeline, a fighting chance. You’re rewarding our resilience. And it will go a long way in making sure that we’re able to offer the care that they need,” she said.

Delivering her remarks, executive director at Sandals Foundation Heidi Clarke spoke of the event’s importance. She said the past three challenges raised £300,000 across Antigua & Barbuda in 2023, Saint Vincent & the Grenadines in 2024, and Saint Lucia in 2025 collectively, benefiting about 1,800 babies.

“I’m very excited to see this finally come home to Jamaica, and as our road to recovery continues here in Jamaica, we know it all too well and [so do] the dedicated teams at the hospitals. It has been a difficult and long road, but with many partners, we’ve been able to work together to make things come to life. We have to recognise, more than ever, the strength of our health care systems are what matter and make communities stronger. Everybody in this room today helps to make events like this possible. And we could not be more grateful,” she said.

Meanwhile, Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett told the launch that the testimonial from McKenzie very nearly moved him to tears, hailing the event as a well-needed lifesaving mechanism.

“The passion that drives the Island Challenge, for example, is a powerful one. Because it’s not just one of physical fitness, discipline, dexterity, agility, and ability to use GPS (global positioning system) to navigate through and find your places. It’s not just about that only. It’s about why you do it…

“In the end, you will say, ‘I’m not here for me. I’m here because of others.’ And so what the foundation is doing is demonstrating practically that we are here for others. And tourism connects others,” said Bartlett.

World.title: ‘Mikie’ Bennett: ‘It was a different kind of excitement’
World.content:
Record producer, composer, vocalist and multi-instrumentalist Mikie BennettKarl Mclarty

The first time Mikie Bennett heard a song he wrote played on the radio he shelved his ambitions of a corporate career. That song was Irons In The Fire, recorded in 1980 by Home T 4, the group in which he was a member.

“I had to pull over. My arms were shaking. It was a thing, like, ‘I want more of this, I need this. This is what I want to live for,’ ” he recalled.

Bennett has lived for music since then, establishing himself as a songwriter/producer for major acts like Dennis Brown, Maxi Priest, Shabba Ranks, Cocoa Tea, and J C Lodge.

His work have been recognised by the Jamaican Government, which has made him a member of the Order of Distinction in the rank of Officer class for his contribution to the music industry.

When he was informed of the national honour, Bennett said two people instantly came to mind — his mother, Ivy Bennett, and his aunt Amy Picart, her sister.

Ivy Bennett was a literature teacher, who encouraged her son to read more, which nurtured his love for writing.

Amy Picart was a librarian with a meticulous nature, who later managed his Grafton recording studio in east Kingston.

Bennett says while he has received music industry awards, it is not on the same level as national recognition.

“When I got the phone call it was a feeling I wasn’t prepared for; it was a different kind of excitement. A wonderful feeling,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

A Kingston College (KC) graduate, Bennett seemed destined for a conventional nine-to-five job after tertiary studies in business administration from West Indies Teachers’ College (now Northern Caribbean University).

But his music career thrived during the 1980s and 1990s, considered by music pundits as the most creative period in dancehall music.

He co-wrote several of that era’s biggest hit songs, including Temptress (Maxi Priest); Housecall, Mr Loverman (Shabba Ranks); Pirates Anthem (Home T, Cocoa Tea, Shabba Ranks); Can You (Brian and Tony Gold); and Telephone Love by J C Lodge.

Bennett was raised in Vineyard Town, a middle-class community. His neighbours included the Chung brothers, Geoffrey and Mikey, who were respected session musicians/producers.

His biggest musical influence, however, was producer Gussie Clarke, another KC old boy who operated the Music Works label and studio.

Bennett credits Clarke with showing him the business side of things, including publishing and the importance of assembling a solid production team.

In the 1990s, Bennett also worked with producers Lloyd “King Jammy” James, Steely and Clevie, and Bobby Digital. Those associations were also invaluable.

“Jammys has golden ears, but the day-to-day guidance came from Bobby Digital. They knew who they were recording music for. They knew the kind of rhythms the people wanted. And they knew the communication style to reach them,” said Bennett. “They also knew how to take a chance with something different.”

Mikie Bennett is one of nine music industry figures who will receive national honour and awards.

Guitarist Earl “Chinna” Smith, singer Stranger Cole (posthumously), producer Robert Livingston, and deejay Mr Vegas, will also receive the OD (Officer Class).

Percussionists Norman “Bongo Herman” Davis and Lawrence “Larry” McDonald; Carlyle Palmer, co-founder of Jet Star Records in the United Kingdom; and Shirley Findley-Willis, are recipients of the Badge of Honour for Meritorious Service.

Though the assignments take effect on Independence Day, August 6, the annual Ceremony of Investiture and Presentation of National Honours and Awards will this year take place on National Heroes’ Day on October 19 at King’s House in St Andrew.

World.title: SHERWIN-WILLIAMS ENDS JAMAICAN MANUFACTURING
World.content:
Sherwin-Williams’ White Marl facility in St Catherine, where the paint company ended manufacturing on July 31, 2026. Products previously made at the plant, including several longstanding lines in the Kem range, will now be manufactured at other Sherwin-Williams facilities overseas and imported into Jamaica. The White Marl distribution centre remains operational as the company moves its Jamaican business to a distribution-focused model. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

SHERWIN-WILLIAMS has called time on more than half a century of paint manufacturing in Jamaica, ending production at its White Marl factory and shifting to imports to supply products that have long rolled off its production lines in St Catherine.

The US paint and coatings giant confirmed to the Jamaica Observer that July 31 was its final day of manufacturing at the facility, ending a production run that began in 1974 and at one point included a full range of automotive, decorative and industrial finishes.

Long-standing products including Kem Flat, Kem Gloss, Kem Low Sheen, and Sherwil Special were among those produced at White Marl. Sherwin-Williams said products previously manufactured there will now be made at other facilities within its international network and imported into Jamaica.

The company, however, declined to say where that production is being moved, leaving unanswered whether Jamaica will be supplied from North America, Latin America or a combination of plants within its global network. It also did not clarify whether all the familiar product lines produced at White Marl will continue to be sold locally.

“Sherwin-Williams confirms that manufacturing operations at its St Catherine facility permanently concluded on July 31, 2026,” the company said in response to questions from the Business Observer.

“Products previously manufactured at St Catherine will be produced at other Sherwin-Williams manufacturing locations and imported into Jamaica, then distributed through our established local supply chain network to Sherwin-Williams stores and other retailers across the island.”

The decision effectively reverses a journey that began more than five decades ago when Sherwin-Williams moved beyond importing and distributing paint in Jamaica and invested in local production.

The company entered Jamaica in the 1960s as a marketing operation, importing products for sale locally and through dealers across the Caribbean. It established the White Marl factory in 1972 and formally began production in 1974.

By 2023, Sherwin-Williams was outlining plans to expand its Jamaican business and sharpening its position against competitors such as Berger, BH and EdgeChem.

At the time, the Business Observer reported that the company had been recording double-digit growth over the previous five years and was continuing to invest in its retail network. Then District Manager Kenneth Richardson said Sherwin-Williams was relying on new products, improved quality and technology to differentiate itself in the market, including in the hotel and hospitality sector.

Technology was also being deployed inside the White Marl factory to scan paint formulas, allowing for faster mixing and production.

“A key part of our strategy is providing the market with products and services that cannot be matched by our competitors,” Richardson said at the time.

The company was also looking beyond Jamaica. While it was already exporting some products to Barbados, Richardson said the immediate priority was to build the Jamaican operation before making a bigger push into the wider Caribbean.

“We know that there is potential in Jamaica but also in the Caricom region. We do some exporting right now to Barbados, but even as we look at the potential outside Jamaica, what we are trying to do first is to continue to grow locally and then expand further out,” Richardson said.

Three years later, Sherwin-Williams has 24 Jamaican stores, up from 23 at the time, but local manufacturing is no longer part of that growth model.

The closure takes on added significance given the role White Marl played in Sherwin-Williams’ wider Caribbean footprint.

The company’s 2025 annual report identifies Jamaica as its only principal manufacturing location in the Caribbean, even as Sherwin-Williams maintains a retail presence across several markets in the region.

At the end of 2025, its Paint Stores Group operated stores in Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, Grenada, Trinidad and Tobago, St Maarten, Jamaica, Curaçao, Aruba, St Lucia, and Barbados.

The closure therefore removes the only Caribbean manufacturing operation identified among the company’s principal facilities in its 2025 annual report, leaving the company with an extensive sales and distribution network in the region but production located elsewhere.

The Jamaican decision also comes as the US parent has been simplifying parts of its wider manufacturing and supply chain operations.

In its 2025 annual report, Sherwin-Williams said its simplification programme was aimed at identifying and eliminating complexities that did not add value. Among the initiatives cited was the consolidation of 14 resin platforms into two and the simplification of more than 500 product formulas.

The company said those changes could help avoid manufacturing capital expenditure, reduce supply risks and simplify manufacturing processes and costs.

Sherwin-Williams also describes its global supply chain, which covers procurement, manufacturing and distribution, as a competitive advantage. During 2025 it continued asset optimisation efforts in Europe, including the rationalisation of three sites.

The company has not said that the White Marl closure formed part of those specific initiatives.

Instead, Sherwin-Williams said the decision reflected its efforts to better organise production across its manufacturing network and improve operational flexibility.

“Sherwin-Williams regularly reviews its business operations to ensure alignment to enterprise priorities and strengthen operational flexibility. Harmonizing production across our manufacturing network enhances our ability to respond quickly to customer and market needs while maintaining high levels of service and product quality,” the company said.

It stressed that the decision was not the result of the performance of the St Catherine factory or its employees and said the closure was not part of a broader announced shutdown of Sherwin-Williams operations across the Caribbean or Latin America.

Twenty-one employees entered consultations related to the closure. Seven were transferred to other positions within the company, while the remaining 14 were separated.

Sherwin-Williams said those workers received all legally required payments along with additional voluntary benefits and resources to assist with their transition.

Despite the end of manufacturing, Sherwin-Williams retains a sizeable Jamaican operation.

The company said it employs approximately 180 people and operates 24 company-owned retail stores, serving more than 27,000 customers through its various sales channels.

Its distribution centre at White Marl will also remain operational, while decommissioning of the manufacturing section is expected to continue into 2027.

The company said that the decommissioning of the manufacturing section would not affect product quality, availability or customer service.

Asked whether replacing locally manufactured products with imports could have implications for prices, particularly with freight, foreign exchange and other import-related costs now forming part of the supply chain, Sherwin-Williams declined to give a projection.

“As a matter of practice, we do not speculate about future pricing, which can be influenced by a range of market and business factors,” the company said.

It said Jamaica nevertheless remains an important market.

“We will continue to invest in our people, stores and distribution network while providing customers with the quality products and dependable service they have come to expect from Sherwin-Williams.”

World.title: JUST CHILL
World.content:
Joseph Salmon of Jamaica celebrates after winning the bronze medal in the men’s discus throw on Sunday’s final day of competition at the World Athletics Under-20 Championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon. Salmon threw 64.37m. (Photo: Paul Reid)

Technical leader of Jamaica’s World Athletics Under-20 team David Riley has hit back at critics of the team’s selection and tactics at the just-concluded championships in Eugene, Oregon, insisting that the decisions made by the coaching and management staff should be respected.

Riley, who was part of the management team that guided Jamaica to eight medals and third place in the placing table, said the performances of the athletes should speak for themselves, pointing to the number of finalists and strong times produced by the team.

“They need to really just chill and understand that the expertise to manage a team is dispatched to the championships,” said Riley upon the team’s arrival on Tuesday at the Norman Manley International Airport.

“They need to respect the judgment and the professionalism of the people who are there,” he added.

“The teams ran well. You can see it from the times that they ran. You can’t run faster than you’ve ever run and it’s a complaint. So we dismiss those and suggest that they be better students of the sport,” said Riley.

Jamaica finished fourth in the medals table with eight medals, inclusive of two gold, three silver, and three bronze. The United States of America topped the table with 24 medals (12 gold, seven silver, and five bronze), finishing ahead of Kenya with 11 medals and Italy in third with five, but their three gold medals put them ahead of Jamaica. Australia rounded out the top five with six medals.

However, Jamaica were third in the Placing Table with 89 points behind the Americans with 218 and Kenya with 92 points. South Africa, with 72 points, were fourth ahead of Japan in fifth on 69 points.

He continued: “We were in a lot of finals and pretty much looked like the Jamaican team of old. Just finding our way, won some medals, but overall it was a strong performance. We were third on the points table, which is usually where we are. We are still a top three nation in the world, so I think it was a good performance,” Riley reiterated.

Jamaica won two gold medals courtesy of team Captain Michael-Andre Edwards, who posted an impressive 17.08m to win the triple jump and the women’s 4×100 team of Sashana Johnson, Theianna-Lee Terrelonge, Natrece East, and Shanoya Douglas, who sped to 42.89, which is the fastest Under-20 time in the world.

Douglas was expected to win triple gold, but she had to settle for two silvers in the 100 and 200 metres behind American rising star Mia Maxwell, while Jamaica’s promising Gary Card had to play second fiddle to the star of the championship, Tate Taylor, who won the sprint double, taking the 100m in a personal best 9.94 (0.1 m/s) and the 200m in a championship record 19.83 (0.1 m/s).

The quartet of Jabari Matheson, Kristen Herbert, Jason Pitter, and Kevongaye Fowler broke ther national Under-20 record in the 4×400 mixed relay but failed to earn a medal.

“We were running 3:18 in the mixed relay and did not medal. We had a national record, which is crazy. We knew we could run 3:18 but never thought we would not get a medal with that kind of time,” Riley noted.

“We used to be 13.2, not making the finals in the sprint hurdles. You realise that, in fact, the performances have really stepped up. We just have to face that reality and work a little harder,” he added.

“I thought we prepared well. The athletes were well prepared. We had a couple of camps. The fact that we made all the relay finals speaks to the fact that the relay camps actually do work. We were the only nation to have made all six relay finals. I think we did well,” he emphasised.

Riley also addressed the concern of Jabari Matheson who ran three races in a 24-hour span, having participated in the heats of the mixed relay before running his individual 400m flat event.

“We gave him the option of running in the finals after the prelims and he wanted to because the team had a shot at the medal. He felt that the team was strong enough with the changes that we were proposing. And the kid wanted a medal, just like the rest of the team wanted a medal,” Riley explained.

“People can make their own statements, but the reality is when you’re on the ground and you talk to athletes…those who want to run and those who don’t want to run, that’s the team that goes out there,” he added.

He also explained the decisions on Shameika McLean, who was Jamaica’s best quarter-miler but missed the 4×400 relays.

“She couldn’t make it. She ran the round of the 400m with a heavily bandaged knee and also in the 4×400 relays heats.

“So she couldn’t make it, and you can’t run a final if you don’t make the prelims. And you can’t be arrogant in your approach to the prelims to say that any team you send out there is going to qualify,” said Riley.

“We don’t want to take that risk. We brought enough persons to the meet with the depth. And we knew we were short in terms of the depth on the female side for the 400m,” he explained.

“We couldn’t find enough girls to run at the trials and to run decent times. So it was always going to be a stretch for us at the 400 based on those who reported to the trials. So there was no second-guessing there.

World.title: Byles accepts blame for JAM-DEX’s slow take-up
World.content:
Outgoing BOJ Governor Richard Byles acknowledges that the central bank’s roll-out strategy contributed to JAM-DEX’s slow take-up. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

FOR every $1,000 in currency issued by Bank of Jamaica (BOJ) at the end of June, less than $1 was in JAM-DEX, underscoring the digital dollar’s limited reach as outgoing Governor Richard Byles accepts that the central bank mishandled parts of its roll-out.

Byles, whose tenure ends on August 18, said BOJ waited about two years before involving commercial banks and should have enlisted the Government from the outset to make digital payments a national priority.

“Let me take some of the blame,” Byles told the Jamaica Observer during an exit interview.

“If I was to do it again, I would ask the Government of Jamaica to work with the Bank of Jamaica to express to the DTIs (deposit-taking institutions) that the business of digital payments is a matter of national interest,” he said.

“It is not just the Bank of Jamaica. It is a national imperative that Jamaica digitises, and the payment system is an important aspect of that.”

JAM-DEX is an electronic version of the Jamaican dollar issued by BOJ and accessed through approved digital wallets. Unlike cryptocurrency, its value does not fluctuate independently. One JAM-DEX dollar is equal to one Jamaican dollar.

At the end of June, BOJ reported $311.34 billion in total currency issue, comprising $303.39 billion in banknotes, $7.66 billion in coins and $290.65 million in JAM-DEX.

The digital currency therefore represented approximately 0.09 per cent of the total — about $1 in JAM-DEX for every $1,070 in currency issued.

The comparison does not measure how often JAM-DEX is spent. The $290.65 million represents the amount issued rather than the total value of transactions, but it illustrates how small JAM-DEX remains compared with physical cash.

BOJ reported 305,026 registered JAM-DEX users at the end of 2025, an increase of 8.1 per cent over the previous year. Registration, however, does not necessarily mean that a wallet is being used regularly.

Of the $260.1 million in JAM-DEX classified as being in circulation at the end of 2025, $144.4 million, or 55.5 per cent, was held by the public. Wallet providers held the remaining $115.7 million in their digital vaults.

BOJ’s published annual figures do not show how many registered wallets are active, how frequently they are used or how much is spent by repeat users. The central bank nevertheless reported increased use during 2025, with acceptance expanding to more restaurants, entertainment businesses and bookstores.

BOJ waited too long

Byles said the central bank spent about two years preparing JAM-DEX before bringing commercial banks into the project.

“We spent about two years in preparing before we went to the banks. I would have brought the banks in from that time so that they could see exactly what we were preparing to do,” he said.

Byles has repeatedly expressed frustration with the time banks have taken to introduce JAM-DEX services. Banks, however, have said implementation requires costly changes to their core computer systems at a time when customer demand remains relatively low.

Byles now acknowledges that BOJ’s approach contributed to the delay. Without a clear national directive, he said, JAM-DEX was forced to compete with other technology projects within financial institutions.

“JAM-DEX was put at number five on the list of that institution and number eight on the list of that institution, because they have other technological imperatives, and I understand that,” he said.

“But had it started in a more important fashion, it would have jumped the queue to being number one or two in all of the DTIs, and I think we would have gone a little farther than we have now.”

Byles said BOJ never expected JAM-DEX to replace cash quickly. The central bank envisaged about five per cent more cash transactions becoming digital each year, which he said meant the transition could take between 10 and 15 years.

Spending remains the obstacle

For Byles, the immediate problem is not the design of JAM-DEX but the limited number of businesses where people can spend it.

“JAM-DEX works,” he said. “JAM-DEX exists and people are doing transactions with the money. I don’t think we need to redesign the model.”

JAM-DEX payments can be made using QR codes, but the point-of-sale machines used by shops, supermarkets and restaurants must be configured to accept them.

“What’s the point of you getting money in JAM-DEX if you can’t go and spend it in restaurants or supermarkets because the POS machines don’t take it?” Byles asked.

Jamaica had 34,151 point-of-sale terminals at the end of 2025, up 7.3 per cent from a year earlier.

Byles estimated that approximately 18,000 machines would need to be adapted to accept JAM-DEX, although it was not immediately clear what portion of the wider network that figure covered.

He reiterated that BOJ was prepared to pay half the cost of upgrading the required machines, describing the contribution as an investment in the national payment system. He said JAM-DEX could be promoted more heavily once it is accepted at significantly more businesses.

The cost of cash

Byles rejected the argument that banks necessarily have an incentive to resist JAM-DEX because it competes with their card-payment services. He argued that reducing Jamaica’s dependence on cash could save banks, businesses and the country money.

Banks must operate and replenish automated teller machines, transport currency and pay for security. Businesses face similar costs to collect, protect and deposit cash, while BOJ spends foreign currency to have Jamaican banknotes and coins manufactured overseas.

“It is a cost to the banks and a cost to business to be managing all of that cash. It is a very expensive thing. And to the country,” Byles said.

“If you knew the kind of US dollars we have to pay to get currency printed, to get coins made to circulate, that is money that we could save by having a digital payment system.”

He said the expenses run into millions of dollars annually but did not provide a precise figure. He also argued that problems with ATMs damage the reputation of banks while adding to their operating costs.

The disruption caused by Hurricane Melissa exposed weaknesses across Jamaica’s payment system. Damage and interruptions to roads, electricity and telecommunications affected access to bank branches, ATMs and electronic payments.

Greater JAM-DEX use could make it easier for people to send money directly to each other and for the Government to make emergency payments, although those services would still require functioning telecommunications networks.

JAM-DEX must also compete with payment methods that Jamaicans already use extensively. During 2025, customers conducted 76.1 million debit-card transactions valued at approximately $1 trillion and 35.1 million credit-card transactions valued at $1.5 trillion.

The challenge is therefore not simply to persuade Jamaicans to use less cash, but to convince them to adopt another form of digital payment alongside cards and bank transfers.

Byles maintains that JAM-DEX is a sound product but concedes that BOJ should have taken a different approach to securing the support of the Government and commercial banks.

Asked what major project remained unfinished as he prepared to leave BOJ, he expressed regret over JAM-DEX’s limited progress.

“I haven’t completed JAM-DEX. For that, I am really sorry, because I think it’s a good product. I think Jamaica needs it,” Byles said.

“It actually exists out there but in small doses, but I think with the power of Government and the cooperation ultimately of the commercial banks, we will get that done.”

World.title: Committing to CCJ would be reckless, says Tavares-Finson
World.content:
Tom Tavares Finson

President of the Jamaican Senate, King’s Counsel Tom Tavares-Finson says it would be extremely reckless for Jamaica to commit to the Caribbean Court of Justice (CCJ) as its final appellate court given the turmoil currently gripping the institution.

The Trinidad Express reported earlier this week a series of allegations made by judges of the CCJ, including allegations of dictatorial tendencies in the running of the court and a series of inter-personal conflict.

Tavares-Finson says no less than a public enquiry is required to deal with the issues facing the CCJ.

While acknowledging that inter-personal conflicts is not unusual for a court, he said the allegation surrounding the convening of panels to achieve pre-desired outcomes is troubling and must be treated seriously.

Tavares-Finson says the Opposition People’s National Party, whose insistence that Jamaica must accept the CCJ as its final appellate court has stalled the island’s constitutional reform process, should state clearly whether it maintains its position despite the turmoil which has gripped the regional court.

World.title: WATCH: 20 families homeless after early morning demolition in Trelawny
World.content:
Flattened structures in Coopers Pen, Trelawny after a demolition crew tore down 20 housing units in the area on Tuesday, August 11, 2026. (Photo: Horace Hines)

TRELAWNY, Jamaica — Some 20 families in Coopers Pen, Trelawny, have been left homeless after a demolition team reportedly tore down about 20 housing units in an early-morning operation Tuesday.

The residents say they have been before the courts since 2009 for the parcel of land that some say they have occupied for more than three decades.

Residents said the demolition crew arrived on the parcel of land shortly after 3:30 am, catching them off guard and leaving little time to save their belongings.

The team reportedly arrived with two excavators, sledgehammers, pickaxes and other equipment, and was accompanied by a strong contingent of police personnel.

Residents said they received no prior warning before the demolition began.

They also claimed that, before leaving the area, members of the demolition team warned that they would return in the coming weeks to continue the operation.

World.title: Eurovision bars countries at war or in ‘sensitive geopolitical situations’ from hosting
World.content:
Despite this, Israel has come close to winning the 2025 and 2026 editions of the competition, garnering a strong public vote. Israel’s pubic broadcaster KAN has denied claims that results were unfairly influenced by mass voting campaigns.

Eurovision is organized by the European Broadcasting Union, an alliance of 113 public service media organizations across 56 countries. Typically, the national broadcaster that wins the competition hosts the following edition in their home country.

There have been some exceptions. When Ukraine won the 2022 contest, the organizers said the country could not host the following year’s contest due to Russia’s ongoing invasion raising safety concerns.

The new rules would make a winning broadcaster automatically ineligible to host “if an armed conflict, a sensitive geopolitical situation, or any other situation materially affects the security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region.”

The organizers could still commission an independent security assessment to determine whether a winner can safely host the contest. If a winner is deemed unable to host, the broadcasting union has the power to choose an alternative.

Organizers said the rule change follows “feedback from participating broadcasters” after the 2026 contest in Vienna. They will apply from next year, when the contest takes place in Bulgaria.

“These changes are about giving everyone involved greater clarity, protecting artists and ensuring the Contest continues to provide a safe and welcoming environment, while preserving the spirit and integrity that make the Eurovision Song Contest so special,” said Eurovision director Martin Green.

World.title: Poland rekindles Musk feud over Starlink snub
World.content:
“Note: Poland is not included in the Europe region above. Accounts registered in Poland are treated as Poland-only for home-country use,” reads Starlink’s current guidance.

Polish Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski also went after Musk, accusing Starlink's parent company SpaceX of treating Poles as second-class customers and demanding it spell out the regulatory basis for the change.

“Poland is not a second-tier market. Polish customers are not second-tier customers,” Gawkowski wrote on X. If SpaceX blames “local regulatory requirements,” Warsaw expects it to point to the specific rules rather than offer “general explanations,” he added.

The new rules have applied to new customers signing up for Starlink since July 14, 2026 and will extend to existing Polish users on Aug. 17.

This isn't the first time Sikorski and Musk have fought over Starlink. Last year, Musk told the Polish minister to “be quiet, small man,” after Sikorski warned that Warsaw could seek alternative providers for the satellite service it's financing for Ukraine.

SpaceX did not immediately respond to POLITICO's request for comment.

World.title: Meta AI glasses face criminal complaint in Germany
World.content:
The complaint, which alleges the sale breaches Germany’s Telecommunications, Digital Services and Data Protection Act, was filed against Meta, Ray-Ban and Oakley — eyewear brands that have partnered with Meta to design the glasses — and several retailers.

Meta spokesperson Matthew Pollard said the smart glasses were approved by Germany's regulator BNetzA in 2022, and “were built with privacy safeguards from the ground up that go beyond what any smartphone offers.” Those include an LED light that turns on when the glasses are recording, as well as technology to stop anyone from tampering with the light.

HateAid said that smart glasses should only be sold if they are clearly identifiable, and that there should be limits on recording in certain spaces as there is for dashcams or bodycams.

Europe's privacy regulators have commissioned a report on smart glasses that is due to be finalized this summer.

World.title: Putin threat pushes Germany to give spies major new powers
World.content:
Germany’s postwar foreign intelligence service was founded in 1956 with far more legal constraints than intelligence agencies elsewhere. Those restraints have had the side effect of making Germany particularly dependent on the U.S. for intelligence gathering.

In view of the growing threat from Russia, leading politicians now argue that it is time for Germany’s spies to be given the ability to hit back harder. That argument took on new urgency following the sighting of an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig-Halle Airport in eastern Germany last week that was found near a Ukrainian Antonov plane used to transport munitions.

Dobrindt, in remarks after the incident, stopped short of naming Russia as responsible for the drone incursion, but said that “a hybrid threat is evident” and that such perils do not originate from amateurs but are “often linked to foreign powers.” On Wednesday, he said results of an investigation into the drone incident were still pending.

Germany’s security “worsened significantly” in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to a report by the country’s domestic intelligence agency last year.

Germany’s intelligence reform would allow authorities to actively respond to hybrid threats such as the Leipzig drone incident. Measures could range from exposing those involved or destroying their property to sabotaging explosives before an attack or feeding adversaries false intelligence afterward, according to the proposed reform. Any response would have to be directly linked to the original incident and could not endanger life or physical safety.

“We are expanding the technical capabilities of the intelligence services and granting them active, operational powers,” Dobrindt said. “This is not just about enabling the services to see and hear better in the future and analyze information more quickly. Above all, it is about being able to take active measures against our attackers and adversaries.”

The BND will also face fewer data-protection restrictions, allowing it to make greater use of tools such as AI and facial recognition and to store data for longer periods of time, according to the proposed reform. The agency is also set to receive more funding in the coming years. Merz’s government increased the agency’s budget by about 26 percent to €1.51 billion this year.

World.title: Ukraine hammers key Russian port in overnight drone attack
World.content:
The Ukrainian president said Kyiv’s forces were attacking a Black Sea naval base, while Russian officials pointed to civilian casualties and destroyed residential buildings.

Russian authorities said Ukraine’s overnight bombardment of the western Krasnodar region killed two people and injured at least 12.

Andrei Kravchenko, mayor of the Russian city Novorossiysk, said the attack killed one child and injured eight people. Drone debris damaged four businesses and 21 residential buildings, including apartment blocks, he said. Krasnodar Krai regional governor, Veniamin Kondratyev, said on his Telegram channel that more buildings were damaged elsewhere in the region, killing one man and injuring four people.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the attack on Wednesday but insisted that Kyiv’s forces had targeted the naval base in Novorossiysk, which he called “the last major stronghold of the Russian fleet in the Black Sea.”

World.title: Die neue Weltordnung der AfD
World.content:

Pauline von Pezold und Frederik Schindler widmen sich in dieser Folge gemeinsam mit Jacob Ross, Research Fellow bei der Deutschen Gesellschaft für Auswärtige Politik , der Außenpolitik der AfD. Sie analysieren gemeinsam mit ihm, wie sich die Partei von einer reinen Protestbewegung zu einer gestaltenden Kraft mit einem eigenen Gegenentwurf zur Außenpolitik der Bundesregierung entwickeln will.

Im Zentrum steht das Konzept der „Multipolarität“. Einer Weltordnung, die in regionale Einflusssphären unterteilt ist, wie sie von Russland und China propagiert und von Teilen der AfD angestrebt wird. Schindler, Ross und von Pezold diskutieren, ob der Versuch der AfD, gleichzeitig die Nähe zu Putins Russland und zum Amerika unter Donald Trump zu suchen, ein Widerspruch ist oder vielmehr Teil einer kohärenten Strategie ist, um sich als neue Kraft in einer veränderten Welt zu positionieren.

Außerdem gehen sie der Frage nach, wie realistisch ein solcher außenpolitischer Kurswechsel für Deutschland wäre.

„Inside AfD“ ist der POLITICO-Podcast über die umstrittenste Partei des Landes. Trotz Radikalisierung und Beobachtung durch den Verfassungsschutz wächst die AfD weiter. Wie ist das möglich? Was treibt ihre Anhänger, Strategen und Gegner an? Wie funktioniert das Innenleben der Partei? Und was bedeutet ihr Aufstieg für das politische System Deutschlands?

Antworten liefern immer mittwochs Pauline von Pezold von POLITICO und Frederik Schindler von WELT — unaufgeregt, aber kritisch.

World.title: Burnham chairs crisis meeting as UK swelters in extreme heat
World.content:
A Downing Street spokesperson said: “We know how challenging this summer is proving, particularly for firefighters tackling wildfires, farmers working in drought conditions, and NHS staff in busy A&E units.

“We will continue to take the action needed to keep communities safe, protect water supplies, support farming communities and safeguard the environment.”

Britons are this week bracing for their fifth heatwave of 2026, with some temperatures forecast to exceed 36C. The Met Office, Britain's national weather service, has warned that this summer is set to be the U.K.'s hottest since records began.

More than two-thirds of England is now in drought after the driest July since records began in 1836. The whole of Wales is also in drought, and more than 27 million people across the U.K. are facing water restrictions including hosepipe bans.

The U.K. is grappling with wildfires including at the New Forest national park in south England. The National Fire Chiefs Council responded to 458 wildfires last month, its busiest month on record.

'Snail's pace'

The rival Green Party first demanded a COBR meeting weeks ago after a wildfire engulfed parts of Suffolk in eastern England. Green Leader Zack Polanski said Wednesday's meeting is “only a first step. This is a climate emergency which is leading to hundreds of deaths and stretching our firefighters, health staff and farmers to the limit. What we urgently need is concrete action.”

World.title: White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt to leave role at end of month, Trump says
World.content:
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, the youngest person to hold the role, will leave at the end of the month, US President Donald Trump announced on Wednesday.

 

Leavitt, 28, the youngest ever US presidential top spokesperson, has been a fiercely loyal Trump defender, delivering fluent and aggressive performances at often combative press briefings.

"Our wonderful White House Press Secretary, and one of my most trusted aides, Karoline Leavitt, will be departing her role at the end of the month so she can spend more time with her beautiful young children and family," Trump said on social media.

He said Leavitt “will be departing her role at the end of the month so she can spend more time with her beautiful young children and family, a decision I totally understand and respect! Karoline will now be one of my top outside advisors, and an influential voice within the Republican Party, as we work to defy History, and conclusively win the Midterm Elections.”

A screenshot of a post on US President Donald Trump's Truth Social account, 12 August, 2026 @realDonaldTrump

Leavitt recently returned to work after taking leave following the birth of her second child, a daughter, in May. She also has a two-year-old son.

"The truth is since returning to the White House after the birth of my daughter, I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary — and that is why I have ultimately made the bittersweet decision to depart the White House and embark on a new chapter in my life,” Leavitt said in a post on X.

Trump did not outline plans for who might replace her in the high-profile role.

Leavitt's departure comes as Trump faces steadily sinking poll numbers and the Republican Party risks defeat in the November midterm congressional elections.

She worked as a spokesperson for MAGA Inc., a super PAC supporting Trump, before joining his 2024 campaign.

In 2022, she ran for Congress in New Hampshire, winning a 10-way Republican primary before losing to incumbent Democratic Representative Chris Pappas.

During Trump’s first term in office, Leavitt worked as a press aide in the White House press office.

She then became communications director for New York Republican Representative Elise Stefanik.

"I have relished holding the liberal media accountable and ensuring the American people hear the truth about President Trump’s successes," she said.
