World.title: Irakli Kobakhidze: “‘Deep state’ is trying to artificially fuel Russophobia in Georgia”
World.content:
“Radical anti-Russian sentiment in the country is being artificially fuelled and is part of a new campaign against Georgia,” Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said at a briefing. He said attempts to intensify Russophobia in Georgia were part of a plan carried out by agents of the “deep state”.

Kobakhidze recalled that the Georgian government had repeatedly said that, after Russia launched its full-scale war against Ukraine in 2022, the so-called “global war party” had tried to draw Georgia into the conflict and open a “second front” in the country.

The prime minister said this “window of opportunity” created an “existential threat” to Georgia and its population. He said calls for Georgia to join international sanctions against Russia soon followed. According to the government, complying with those demands would have had serious consequences for the country’s economy.

“Because the Georgian government refused to comply with these demands, pursued a sovereign policy and acted in the interests of the state, our country became a target for the European bureaucracy and Western leaders working in tandem with informal oligarchic forces,” Kobakhidze said.

He also addressed the sanctions imposed by Western countries on the Georgian government. According to Kobakhidze, pressure mechanisms, including sanctions, were already being used when the previous US administration under Joe Biden was in power.

Kobakhidze said the sanctions had targeted senior Georgian government officials, ruling party honorary chairman Bidzina Ivanishvili, judges, senior police officers and others.

He said the West had also used Georgia’s EU membership prospects as a tool to pressure the government.

“They failed to break the ruling party, which enjoys the support of the Georgian people, so now they are trying to use their agents to drag Georgia into a new provocation,” he added.

Kobakhidze said a “new stage of the attack” on Georgia, its people and its sovereignty had begun:

“This is a qualitatively new stage of the attack on Georgia, the Georgian people and the country’s sovereignty, unfolding simultaneously on several fronts.”

Background

Several days before the anniversary of the August 2008 war, Irakli Kobakhidze published a lengthy letter addressing the issue of “Russophobia”.

In the letter, Kobakhidze discussed the links between Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Georgia’s domestic political situation and the opposition’s position. He said the “global war party” benefited from the ongoing conflict in Ukraine because it wanted to “fuel Russophobia at the highest level among its agents around the world, including in Georgia”.

Kobakhidze accused the opposition and civil society of changing their attitude towards Russia. He described their current tough stance towards Moscow as “Russophobia”.

The letter reignited political disputes over the events of the 2008 war. This time, however, the debate focused not only on the circumstances that led to the war and Russia’s responsibility. The prime minister shifted the focus from Russia’s actions to the position of his Georgian opponents.

Georgian PM on “Russophobia”

World.title: Ilham Aliyev’s AzTV interview during Nakhchivan visit: industrial park, energy projects and Zangezur Corridor
World.content:
Ilham Aliyev’s visit to Nakhchivan

On 11 August, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev and First Vice-President Mehriban Aliyeva visited the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic. It was Aliyev’s 17th visit to Nakhchivan since he became president.

During the visit, officials held foundation-laying ceremonies and opened several facilities. Aliyev also visited historical sites and presented battle flags to military units.

The visit ended with an interview with Azerbaijan Television (AzTV), in which Aliyev outlined his plans for Nakhchivan’s development.

The interview focused on the autonomous republic’s economic and social development, energy security and transport infrastructure. Aliyev also discussed Nakhchivan’s place in Azerbaijan’s broader strategy, particularly its future development in conjunction with Karabakh and Eastern Zangezur, territories that came under Baku’s control after the Second Karabakh War.

Key events during the visit

During the visit to Nakhchivan, President Ilham Aliyev and First Lady Mehriban Aliyeva inspected work at the Shams-1 and Garbi Ufug solar power plants, which have a combined capacity of 50 MW.

One of the key events was the laying of the foundation stone for the Nakhchivan Industrial Park. It will be Azerbaijan’s second-largest industrial park by area, after the Sumgayit Industrial Park. A 300 MW thermal power plant is also planned for the site.

Nakhchivan’s total generating capacity currently stands at around 200 MW. Once the new plant comes online, this will increase by roughly half.

The visit programme also included:

the opening of the Nakhchivan Regional DOST Centre;

the presentation of new electric buses and an inspection of railway infrastructure reconstruction works;

the laying of the foundation stone for the Nakhchivan hotel complex, which is expected to be completed by around 2028;

the laying of the foundation stone for a social housing complex;

an inspection of restoration work at the Momine Khatun Mausoleum and the unveiling of a monument to architect Ajami Nakhchivani;

the presentation of Nakhchivan’s General Development Plan through 2044, which envisages expanding the city and increasing its population;

the presentation of battle flags to new commando units of the Separate Combined Arms Army.

Key points from the AzTV interview

Aliyev described his visit to Nakhchivan as a “sign of the autonomous republic’s comprehensive development”. He said every visit should produce concrete results. He highlighted strengthening defence capabilities, energy security, job creation, preserving historical and cultural heritage, and developing transport links as key priorities.

Defence and governance

Aliyev said Nakhchivan’s geographical position – particularly its lack of a direct land connection with mainland Azerbaijan – requires special attention to the region’s defence. He highlighted the creation of the Separate Combined Arms Army and new commando units as key steps.

According to the president, “Azerbaijan’s Armed Forces carry weight in the region”. He also said Nakhchivan had introduced a system of special presidential representatives, similar to the model used in Karabakh and Eastern Zangezur. Aliyev said the benefits of this system of governance were already becoming apparent.

Energy

Nakhchivan has been fully supplied with gas for around 15 years, Aliyev said, thanks to a gas swap agreement with Iran.

The president also placed particular emphasis on the region’s solar energy potential. He said Nakhchivan was Azerbaijan’s most favourable region for solar power generation. More than 600 hectares of land have already been allocated for the development of this sector. The potential is estimated at at least 500 MW and could reach 1 GW in the future.

Aliyev also highlighted the growing role of the private sector. Projects to build solar power plants with a combined capacity of 50 MW are already under way.

The president described electricity exports as a strategic priority. Iran and Turkey are currently the main destinations, but Azerbaijan ultimately hopes to export electricity from Nakhchivan to the European market as well.

Zangezur Corridor – TRIPP

Aliyev said that “the creation of the Zangezur Corridor was our initiative”, recalling that connecting mainland Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan, an integral part of the country, had remained one of Baku’s strategic goals for many years.

He said he had insisted that a provision on the corridor be included in the trilateral statement signed by Azerbaijan, Russia and Armenia on 10 November 2020. Aliyev claims the Armenian side did not want to agree to this, but had no other alternative because continuing the war was not in its interests.

Noting that there had been no practical progress on the issue for five years, Aliyev said a solution emerged after the Washington summit on 8 August 2025, when the TRIPP project (Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity) was launched.

Speaking about the current state of the work, the president said the Horadiz-Aghband highway was almost complete, with only minor technical issues remaining. He said construction of the railway was also progressing rapidly.

Aliyev added that a project for power transmission lines linking mainland Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan through Armenia had already been prepared, and locations for the pylons had been identified.

Aliyev predicted that these projects would eventually turn Nakhchivan into one of the region’s key transport and energy hubs.

A unified development concept

The president stressed that Nakhchivan, Eastern Zangezur and Karabakh should develop under a unified concept. He said the geographical proximity of the three regions requires a common approach to their development.

Aliyev noted that master plans for cities in the territories that came under Azerbaijan’s control after the Second Karabakh War had already been approved. He also said he had ordered the preparation of a similar document for Nakhchivan. The “Nakhchivan City Development Master Plan through 2044” was presented to the president during the current visit.

Speaking about the region’s tourism potential, Aliyev said Nakhchivan had significant opportunities thanks to its rich historical heritage, scenic landscapes and clean air. At the same time, he acknowledged that the hotel infrastructure remained underdeveloped and that the existing hotels were generally of a low standard, hindering the growth of tourism.

He said that to address the problem, construction had begun on a new five-star hotel complex in the city centre. The project is expected to be completed around 2028.

Ilham Aliyev’s visit to Nakhchivan

World.title: Child seats, rear-seat seat belts and alcohol interlocks: changes to Georgia’s traffic rules
World.content:
New road safety rules in Georgia

Georgia plans to tighten road safety rules under the National Road Safety Strategy for 2026–2030, approved by the government on 5 August 2026. The strategy includes changes in several areas.

At this stage, the measures remain proposals, and some will require further legislative amendments before they can take effect.

What is changing:

Child seats will become mandatory for pre-school children. This means that when transporting a child of the relevant age, it will no longer be enough simply to seat them in the car or secure them with a standard seat belt.

This means that when transporting a child of the relevant age, it will no longer be enough simply to seat them in the car or secure them with a standard seat belt. Rear-seat seat belts could become mandatory. The government strategy provides for mandatory seat-belt use by passengers sitting in the back. However, authorities must first establish the necessary legal framework and an enforcement mechanism.

The government strategy provides for mandatory seat-belt use by passengers sitting in the back. However, authorities must first establish the necessary legal framework and an enforcement mechanism. Drunk drivers could be prevented from driving. The strategy provides for the introduction of so-called “alcohol interlocks”. Georgia plans to establish a standard for alcohol-based ignition interlock systems. Under the strategy, authorities intend to take alcohol interlock technology into account when setting requirements for vehicles entering the Georgian market. The strategy does not, however, call for the immediate installation of such devices in all vehicles in the country. Measures to detect drivers under the influence of drugs will be strengthened. No specific new rules have been announced at this stage, although additional regulation remains under consideration. More attention will be paid to pedestrian safety, including children’s safety. The strategy calls for road safety to be incorporated into pre-school education programmes and for educational materials to be developed for parents and children. Future infrastructure projects are expected to give greater consideration to the safety of people with disabilities.

The government strategy says seat-belt use is one of the key ways to reduce deaths and serious injuries in road accidents. It pays particular attention to rear-seat seat belts because unrestrained passengers in the back can endanger not only themselves but also people sitting in the front of the vehicle.

The strategy is not limited to introducing new requirements. The government also plans to raise awareness of road safety, run public campaigns and educational programmes, and improve technical tools for detecting violations.

It is important to note that the government strategy sets out some of these measures only in broad terms. Where necessary, authorities will have to introduce additional legislative and regulatory amendments to implement specific commitments.

World.title: Lasha Bugadze becomes first modern Georgian writer whose book was barred from being sent to prison
World.content:
Precedent for literary censorship in Georgia

The administration of Rustavi Prison refused to allow Lasha Bugadze’s new novel, The Observer, to be delivered to the prison. The book was intended for Nana Sander, who was convicted over her participation in a protest on 4 October 2025.

Notably, the penitentiary code contains no provision explicitly banning fiction from being brought into prisons.

The book’s synopsis describes a fictional political reality involving the long rule of a “despot”, the “division of the country into zones” and a “cult of the leader”. It also mentions the scheduling of elections and a decision by the country’s population on whether they should take place.

According to Bugadze, a prison official refused to allow the book in, saying the novel contained “political content”.

The writer says it is unclear to him who determined that the book contained political content and what criteria they used. He suspects the decision may have been prompted by words and phrases in the novel, such as “despot” and “cult of the leader”.

“The employee told me directly that the book could not be delivered because it was political in nature. I don’t think he sat down and read the book. I doubt he even read the synopsis,” Bugadze said.

In his view, someone appears to have judged the work to be political without giving any clear reason.

“Who put this label on the text? [Who decided] whether it was political or not? What does that even mean? And, excuse me, even if the content is political, why should a citizen – whether a prisoner or anyone else – not have the right to read such a book?” the writer said.

Bugadze sees the incident as a potential precedent for censoring literary works:

“It can be described as the first significant example of literary censorship in modern Georgian history. This is an extremely dangerous precedent, and under no circumstances should it be considered normal. The situation requires a response. No one has the right to stop someone from reading.”

The head of the human rights organisation Sapari, Baia Pataraia, announced that legal proceedings would begin over the incident:

“We are taking legal steps. <…> First, we will demand a written and reasoned refusal.”

The organisation PEN Georgia also responded to the case. It described the incident as an alarming precedent for censorship of a literary work, linked not only to the novel’s content but also to the author’s political and civic stance. The organisation stressed that censoring fiction and restricting freedom of expression are unacceptable in a democratic society.

Lasha Bugadze’s The Observer

Precedent for literary censorship in Georgia

World.title: Armenia seeks alternatives amid concerns over possible Russian gas price hike
World.content:
Russian gas pressure on Armenia

If the issue of raising gas tariffs arises, the Armenian authorities will discuss it with their Russian counterparts in a friendly atmosphere, Sargis Khandanyan, an MP from the ruling Civil Contract faction, told journalists.

Khandanyan added that he had no information about any negotiations with Russia over gas tariffs. However, he expressed confidence that, if necessary, Armenia would be able to find alternatives to Russian gas. These could include supplies from Iran, although this is not the only option.

Yerevan and Tehran have already discussed the issue. Following talks held with Iranian partners by Armenia’s Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure, Davit Khudatyan, it emerged that the volume of Iranian gas supplies could potentially be doubled.

“This decision has nothing to do with any other country, Russia in particular. It is a profitable economic activity that both countries are interested in expanding,” the Armenian minister said.

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan notes that there has recently been increasingly frequent talk of a possible revision of Russian gas prices. He views the issue in the context of the levers of pressure being used against Armenia. In his view, Moscow has already exhausted much of its arsenal and is now resorting to economic leverage, including in the energy sector.

“Political, cultural and terrorist levers, as well as the influence of the criminal subculture, are no longer working for various reasons. And Russia, in order to prevent Armenia from strengthening its independence, has decided to make full use of its last remaining lever,” Ghevondyan said.

‘This scenario cannot be ruled out’: On gas imports from Azerbaijan

Journalists asked MP Sargis Khandanyan how likely it was that the tariff on gas imports from Russia could change by the end of the year.

“I am not aware of when this issue was last discussed with Russia. Nor am I aware of any information that would give grounds to believe that the gas tariff could change,” he replied.

At the same time, the MP noted that the government attaches great importance to diversifying supplies. He recalled the agreements reached during the visit of Armenia’s Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure to Iran. According to him, the “Trump Route” could also be considered as one such opportunity:

“As part of the transit route that will connect Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan through Armenian territory, a gas pipeline will be built. This could provide another opportunity. We could consider this pipeline as an additional source. Of course, this is a very theoretical idea, but it would not be difficult to implement.”

Asked about the possibility of importing gas from Azerbaijan, Khandanyan said that Yerevan and Baku were discussing a broad range of issues:

“I do not know how far we have progressed on the issue of gas supplies, but this scenario cannot be ruled out.”

In late October 2025, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev announced that all restrictions on transit to Armenia would be lifted. Since then, Armenia has been receiving petroleum products from the neighbouring country by rail. According to official figures, Azerbaijan has already supplied Armenia with 20,000 tonnes of petroleum products.

Yerevan and Tehran agree to increase gas supplies. Can Moscow stand in the way?

Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure Davit Khudatyan paid a three-day visit to Iran. Upon returning from Tehran, he said that the volume of Iranian gas supplied under the “Gas for Electricity” programme could be at least doubled. He explained that the pipeline’s capacity exceeds the volume of gas currently being supplied.

Under the programme, Armenia has been receiving gas from Iran since 2009, converting it into electricity which is then supplied back to Iran.

To increase gas imports and export a corresponding volume of electricity to Iran, construction of the Iran-Armenia high-voltage power transmission line needs to be completed. The Armenian government hopes that the long-delayed project will be completed by the end of the year.

Meanwhile, since 2015, the Armenian section of the pipeline carrying gas from Iran has been controlled by Russian company Gazprom.

As a result, some experts doubt whether Iranian gas supplies can be increased without Moscow’s consent. The Armenian government, however, has assured that there will be no obstacles to expanding supplies under the “Gas for Electricity” programme.

Expert commentaty

Political commentator Artem Yerkanyan says:

“Russian Security Council Deputy Secretary Alexei Shevtsov threatened that unless Armenia revises its foreign policy course, it will have to pay $800 for Russian gas instead of the current $177. Compensating for that difference would cost at least $1bn. That is more than the €50m the European Union has promised Armenia as compensation for the impact of strained relations with Russia.

It is worth explaining what the figures of $177 and $800 actually mean. Russia’s Gazprom sells gas for $177 to Gazprom Armenia, which is owned by Gazprom itself. In other words, it also earns revenue from the distribution of the gas, and that revenue also goes to Gazprom. Therefore, I think it would be incorrect to say that Armenia buys gas for $177.

It is also unclear where the figure of $800 comes from, considering the following:

China buys Russian gas for $258;

Turkey for $280;

Hungary, Serbia and Slovakia for $400;

Spain, France and Belgium for $450.

Moreover, according to a forecast by Russia’s Ministry of Economic Development, by the end of this year the average price at which Russia will sell gas to countries outside the EAEU [an economic bloc led by Russia] will be $290.

If the average price is $290, why are they planning to sell it to Armenia for $800? That is unclear.”

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan argues:

“Following the elections, the Armenian authorities have continued to pursue a multi-vector foreign policy. Dependence on Russia is steadily declining, with the economic dimension playing an increasingly important role in this process.

While Russia is trying to exert economic pressure, Armenia is opening up new markets that Armenian businesses previously ‘failed to notice’ because of their excessive focus on the Russian market. Although problems remain with some goods, economic diversification is advancing rapidly.

In the energy sector, Armenia has alternatives when it comes to building a new nuclear reactor, which in itself is a headache for Russia.

It is no coincidence that, alongside economic blackmail, Rosatom executives periodically make Armenia ‘attractive’ offers to build a new Russian nuclear reactor. However, the Armenian authorities are likely to opt for a different proposal.

A rise in gas prices could initially cause problems. But Armenia has alternatives here as well: Iranian, Turkmen and now Azerbaijani gas.

Consequently, in the near future, Russian gas may find itself merely competing on the market. This would limit the Kremlin’s ability to use gas prices to blackmail Armenia.

In conclusion, it should be noted that increased pressure from Russia is having the opposite effect. Armenia is steadily ‘freeing itself’ from excessive Russian influence and diversifying its economy. The Kremlin does not appear to recognise this yet, but that is its problem.”

World.title: Kobakhidze: Georgia does not publicly declare Russia an enemy because this would require follow-up steps
World.content:
Georgian prime minister on Russia

Georgian Dream Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze told journalists that the Georgian government does not publicly call Russia an “enemy” because such a political statement would require corresponding action.

A journalist asked Kobakhidze whether the Georgian government considers Russia an enemy. The prime minister replied:

“Your questions are shameful, you look ridiculous. Let me explain in simple terms why this question is shameful: you want to get a sensational headline, even in the Russian media, saying that I have declared the Russian Federation an enemy. This is a specific political statement that would have to be followed by specific steps – roughly the same, or exactly the same, as those your party” (referring to the United National Movement – JAMnews) “took in 2008 and before.”

The journalist asked whether this was precisely why the government was reluctant to openly call Russia an enemy.

“Of course. What, should I repeat it again?!” Kobakhidze replied.

Kobakhidze also addressed Russia’s occupation of Georgian territories and reiterated that the Russian Federation occupies 20% of Georgia’s territory.

“Of course, the Russian Federation is the only state and party that has occupied Georgian territories. This is an absolutely clear fact. Numerous statements have been made about this, and there is no doubt about it,” Kobakhidze stressed.

He said Russia’s occupation of Georgian territory was a “crime against the Georgian state and the Georgian people”:

“This is an egregious crime: first the occupation, and then the so-called recognition.”

Georgian prime minister on Russia

World.title: 'Back to the 60s' as ombudsman finds systemic issues in telco services
World.content:
Living on the Princes Highway on the NSW South Coast, Gerry McLaughlin's reception can be patchy but when it does drop out he can still call Triple Zero (000).

So it came as a shock earlier this year when he spotted a new symbol on the signal section on his phone, accompanied by a text message from Telstra informing him it was operating in satellite mode.

Do you know more about this or have a similar story? Email pezet.lauren@abc.net.au or laurenpezet@proton.me

"It said this function only has the ability to send text messages, move to an area of mobile coverage if you need to ring Triple Zero," he said.

"First off, I thought: 'Where am I going to drive? Where do you go to get mobile coverage in the event of emergency?'"

Gerry McLaughlin was horrified to learn a new satellite option on his phone meant he could not call Triple Zero. (Supplied: Gerry McLaughlin)

Published maps show Mr McLaughlin's Conjola property should have good coverage across all networks, so under Triple Zero custodian laws if his Telstra service was not available he should expect to be able to access another available network to make an emergency call.

With his phone now instead switching to text only satellite he was concerned a call might no longer be an option, especially given he is in a bushfire-prone area that was razed during the Black Summer bushfires.

"I rang them up and they told me that if you need emergency service, just text a friend and get them to call it."

Claims mobile coverage maps inaccurate Telcos were forced to publish new mobile phone coverage maps last month, but some Telstra customers say they still do not reflect reality.

He contacted the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman to seek a resolution, but he said he never received a straight answer.

Telstra declined to be interviewed but in a statement to the ABC a spokesperson said: "Being connected to Telstra satellite does not stop a compatible device from using another available mobile network to make a Triple Zero call."

Mr McLaughlin was one of 27,000 regional Australians that took their frustrations to the ombudsman over the past two years, with a report released today showing consumers in those areas continue to face major challenges.

Ombudsman Cynthia Gebert said in the regions, "losing connectivity isn't just an inconvenience".

"It can mean that they're unable to call for help in an emergency, stay connected for the purposes of farming equipment or just the internet generally and stay in touch with families," she said.

Cynthia Gebert is the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman. (Supplied: Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman)

Ms Gebert said isolation and a lack of competition meant "the safety risks are more amplified" in the regions compared to similar issues experienced by metro consumers.

"That leaves people vulnerable to service failures, technology changes and rising costs."

'Back to the 60s'

Common themes identified in the report include significant delays in connections and repairs, confusion around the ability to call Triple Zero in some areas, and onerous requirements around identification and requirements to visit physical stores.

Ms Gebert said for many customers, the 3G shutdown in 2024 has also had an ongoing impact.

"We heard from some consumers who have gone back to UHF radios, for example, just to make sure that they can continue to have a reliable way of communicating with other people," she said.

" There's a quote in there that someone says they feel like they've gone back to the 60s, it's not what you expect in 2026. "

Blackspots and failed phone calls It has been more than 80 days since Telstra and Optus flicked the switch on the 3G mobile network. Hundreds of regional and remote Australians say they can no longer rely on the network and struggle to make calls.

Other examples included a man who made three separate 350 kilometre round trips in an attempt to purchase a new handset from a store.

On two of those occasions he was told beforehand that it was ready to be picked up, which turned out not to be true and as such he was left without a phone.

In Western Australia a 90-year-old woman living alone in an area without mobile service reported that her landline, which also supported her medical alarm, was not working.

The issue remained unresolved despite multiple attempts to contact her telco, and came at a time when she had a medical emergency and was unable to call for help.

"One that really stuck out was a consumer that had to wait five months for a connection after 20 cancelled technician appointments and several appointments that went ahead and failed to connect," Ms Gebert said.

" I can't think of many worlds where that would be considered reasonable. "

'Root and branch review' recommended

In addition to 11 specific recommendations, the report made an overarching key recommendation the federal government "conduct a root and branch review of the telecommunications regulatory framework".

Ms Gebert acknowledged there have already been several reviews and reports by various agencies and committees on this issue in recent years, and another one currently being led by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission.

"There is some really good content in those reviews and reports … things that haven't been actioned, that if actioned in a really sensible, not piecemeal, but really sensible way, would deliver improved outcomes for rural, regional and remote consumers," she said.

'Critical' tech help service loses funding If you're having connectivity issues, one place you can turn to is the Regional Tech Hub. But now it might be forced to close.

The specific recommendations include ensuring timely access to technicians for installation and repairs, modernising identification requirements, and developing an independent database similar to the US National Broadband Map that shows what services are available in a particular area.

The report acknowledged that the federal government is introducing Universal Outdoor Mobile Obligation (UOMO) legislation to mandate minimum mobile service requirements, but suggested it could be improved by strengthening protections and compensation for consumers experiencing unreasonable delays.

The Independent Member for Indi, Helen Haines, has been working with the government on amendments to the UOMO bill, including fault rectification time frames, which she said was backed up by the "damning" report.

Helen Haines has been working to introduce amendments to the federal government's Universal Outdoor Mobile Obligation bill. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"We know that if you live outside of a metropolitan area you've got to wait longer to get faults repaired and this has direct material implications for people's quality of life and safety," she said.

"Things like power backup to mobile phone towers during emergency situations such as bushfires, floods, emergency events is a cause for enormous concern and again needs fixing."

Ms Haines said while she "could see a need" for an overarching review there was enough evidence from other reports to push ahead.

"I want to see those immediate and urgent recommendations in regard to service delivery and reliability acted on because we've got solutions that could go to that immediately."

In a statement a government spokesperson pointed to the UOMO bill it has before parliament, amendments currently with the Senate to make industry codes enforceable, and the Triple Zero Legislative and Regulatory Review that is currently underway.

A Telstra spokesperson said they agreed the framework should be reviewed so that it "remained fit for the future".

"As demand for connectivity continues to grow, it's important that regulatory settings encourage investment, strengthen resilience and support innovation across the sector," they said in a statement.

World.title: Bazball-era curfews over as Root demands England players 'be adults'
World.content:
England skipper Joe Root says the midnight curfews in place at the end of the Bazball reign have been ditched as he called on his players to "be adults" in the new era.

With another Ashes series on the horizon in England next summer, Root has launched his second spell as Test captain with the message that his team need to remember: "You're playing for England."

Root's new reign at the age of 35 starts at Headingley next Wednesday against Pakistan in a three-Test series, which will be the first since Ben Stokes retired from international cricket and Brendon McCullum lost his job as Test coach in a turbulent spell.

Stokes claims cricket has drinking culture Ben Stokes defends his former teammates by saying the sport of cricket as a whole has an unhealthy relationship with alcohol.

In an interview with former captain Mike Atherton on Sky Sports Cricket Podcast, Root was asked if the player curfew, which was breached by Stokes and quick Gus Atkinson in a post-midnight nightclub incident in June, was still going to be in place.

"There's not going to be a curfew. I don't think this needs to be a big deal, to be honest," Root said.

"My view on curfews is I don't think they work, and if you want guys to take responsibility on the field they've got to be able to feel they can be grown adults off it and make good strong decisions off it.

"That's for us as a team to manage well, and self-police well, for me and Flem (new coach Stephen Fleming) to manage well in many ways.

Ben Stokes's retirement a perfect example of his main character energy Ben Stokes has been the centre of England's cricketing universe for 15 years. In announcing his retirement mid-match, he highlighted how damaging that main character energy can be.

"But ultimately you're grown adults, you know what it takes to play for England, you know what your responsibilities are off the field, and we need to make sure we don't find ourselves with any little situations off the field.

"We should be known for how we play our cricket and what we do on the field. We should be on the back pages of the newspapers and people reading about that sort of stuff.

"Be adults, look after yourselves, look after each other, create a good strong culture when you know when the right time is to celebrate and enjoy a win or to have a sensible beer or whatever, but remember you're playing for England."

The curfew had been instituted by England men's managing director Rob Key in the aftermath of the pre-Ashes tour to New Zealand last November when Harry Brook was fined for an altercation with a nightclub bouncer on the eve of an ODI in Wellington.

England players' behaviour was then put under the spotlight during their 4-1 Ashes hammering, with opener Ben Duckett admitting he was not proud of being caught on camera under the influence of alcohol when they were 2-0 down in the series.

AAP

World.title: 'Where is our morality?' Holocaust survivor's warning to Australians
World.content:
For decades, the voices of Holocaust survivors have fostered vital conversations about antisemitic atrocities.

One of those survivors is Mark Spigelman, a retired surgeon, professor and medical archaeologist, who volunteers at the Sydney Jewish Museum.

"When the students ask to hear my stories, I explain to them that I don't have that many memories of events, I have nightmares of events," he said.

A story of survival

Born in Poland in 1940, Mr Spigelman was taught to open his blue eyes, smile, never cry, and to only speak German.

He was also taught that in public, he was to appear as a girl.

"The Jewish faith requires that all baby boys be circumcised, so when the Germans were hunting for Jews, the first thing they would do was pull down the pants of young boys," he said.

"That is why I spent most of the war years dressed as a girl."

Mr Spigelman (left) dressed as a girl, next to his grandfather Jacob and cousin, both of whom died in Auschwitz months later. (Supplied)

Inspired by their grandchildren's curiosity to understand more about Mr Spigelman's childhood, his wife Rachel wrote a book for young readers to introduce them to the Holocaust.

In the book, Mr Spigelman references a memory where he and his mother were confronted by German officers. He recounted his mother saying to him in that moment: "Just smile and open your blue eyes, my little girl."

When Mr Spigelman and his parents were liberated on January 27, 1945, they had been hiding on a farm very close to Auschwitz.

"My crazy family thought that was safer than being far away from the camp, because they thought the Germans would never search a farm so close, because no Jew would be so stupid as to hide there. But my parents were right."

When Mr Spigelman went to school in Poland for the first time soon after his family's liberation, he was told he could "play". He had no idea what that meant.

"I spent four years of my life not talking to anyone … I hardly came across another child, because we were hiding."

Mr Spigelman often reflects on his story with high school students. (ABC News: Marcus Stimson)

On his first day in the school yard, he was set upon.

"I was surrounded by a group of Polish kids who started hitting me, saying, 'Jew, you started the war'. I didn't understand what they were talking about."

In Mr Spigelman's hometown of Będzin, there were approximately 60,000 people before World War II, about 30,000 of which were Jewish.

When the war ended, there were just three Jewish children who had survived, Mr Spigelman said.

The next time Mr Spigelman properly went to school again was in 1949 in Sydney's east after he, his parents and his brother James Spigelman AC arrived in Australia as refugees.

"In the schoolyard, my peers came up to me and said, 'Hey mate, tell us about yourself. Do you know how to play cricket?' "I told them I didn't know. "They replied, 'Come on mate we'll show you what to do.' Once you become a mate in Australia, you're set."

He knows firsthand how hatred can morph into something evil. (ABC News: Marcus Stimson)

'I'm worried about my country'

Mr Spigelman enjoys being asked questions by students.

He is not sure if he is changing hearts and minds by telling his story. But he hopes so.

"All I know is that if I don't do it, then no minds will be changed … I've got three grandchildren. I don't want them to go through what I did," he said.

" I'm trying to the prevent the poison of hate from infiltrating into kids. "

Mr Spigelman pictured at a Sydney Jewish Museum event. (Supplied: Sydney Jewish Museum)

Amid the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion and recent events, Mr Spigelman acknowledged it had been a tough time for the Jewish community.

"I'm worried about my country," he said.

"I always had pride in this, Australia as a multicultural society. Where is our morality? Our humanity?"

In the 1990s, Mr Spigelman volunteered at the Sydney Jewish Museum, before then embarking on a career in research and medicine overseas, returning to Australia permanently in 2020.

The museum in Sydney's east has educational programs for school groups. (ABC News: Millie Roberts)

He saw no better time than to restart his volunteer talks at the museum, where he now mostly talks to high school students.

"I've always felt the need to speak to children, because I think children need to be shown good and evil for what it is," he said.

The museum in inner Sydney is closed this year for redevelopment, however, its educational programs for school groups have continued off-site.

It regularly has upward of 50,000 visitors per annum, about 30,000 of those being students who attend specifically for education programs.

For high school students, there are a range of curriculum-linked workshops. (Supplied: Sydney Jewish Museum)

Senior educator Ilana McCorquodale pictured with primary school aged students. (Supplied: Sydney Jewish Museum)

Programs range from interactions with a Holocaust survivor, an analysis on the role of historical fiction texts, and talks on the rise of Nazism in Germany prior to World War II.

Each of the age-appropriate programs invites students to think deeply about Jewish history and identity, with the hope to help stamp out the rise of antisemitism.

As one student told the royal commission, she noticed a positive change in some students' behaviour after a school trip to the Sydney Jewish Museum.

'An upstander of character strengths'

Block six of the royal commission considered the role of education in enhancing social cohesion and tackling hate.

Melbourne Holocaust Museum CEO Breann Fallon gave evidence, calling for a national minimum standard for Holocaust education in the Australian curriculum.

Breann Fallon gave evidence during block six of the antisemitism royal commission.

She pointed to a particular age appropriate program of theirs where students hear the experiences of children that survived the Holocaust in hiding, thanks to the kindness of others.

"It is a remarkable program whereby students learn in particular about that importance of being an upstander of character strengths … bravery, hope, courage, kindness, fairness, perspective and good judgement," she said.

"I remember last year we had a year six student who was going back down the stairs to the bus and she turned around to her teacher and said, 'Every Victorian should have to come here'."

Mr Spigelman wants Australians to remember their morality and humanity. (ABC News: Marcus Stimson)

For Mr Spigelman, he wants the curriculum to focus on addressing racism overall, and then use antisemitism as an example of such hate.

"I keep thinking if children become antisemitic, racist, it makes it easier for them to pick on the next group, after the Jews. No one is immune.

"I want us to return to the days of when I was the new refugee kid in the schoolyard at Maroubra, and they taught me cricket and showed humanity.

"If we return to those principles, we'll have a wonderful country."

World.title: Revived NT mine to join Australia's modern gold rush
World.content:
A third Northern Territory mine is preparing to enter Australia's modern-day gold rush, with the soaring gold price attracting a Chinese-financed company to revive the mothballed Mount Bundy mine near Darwin.

Executives from Hanking Gold visited the mine 100 kilometres south of Darwin this week to turn the first sod for construction of the mine's new gold processing plant.

Hanking Gold chief executive Mark Qiu said the company was confident it could make the operation profitable in the same year it started production, which is planned for the first quarter of 2028.

Mark Qiu expects the mine to run for 17 years. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"We expect profits in the first year, 2028," he said.

"We expect it will be profitable because the gold price at the moment is very high, and with this current price it's a highly profitable project."

Exploration companies cash in on modern-day gold rush The surge in Australian dollar gold prices in the past year is being reflected across regional Western Australia, where gold exploration has hit record levels.

Dr Qiu said Hanking Gold had been planning the project for 12 years, and over that time the company had increased its estimate of the gold resource by 11 times.

"On today's price, it's worth more than $6 billion," he said.

"Our current mine life is 17 years.

"I'm pretty sure we will increase our estimates of the resource and be able to extend that to more than 20 years."

He said the company's feasibility plans judged the project would be profitable with a gold price of $3,750 an ounce.

Hanking Gold will remove all of the old infrastructure from the former operation at Mount Bundy. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

When the old Mount Bundy mine financially collapsed in 1997 after just a decade of intermittent mining, the gold price was $600 an ounce.

In contrast, gold prices this year have remained above $6,000 AUD an ounce.

"Clearly the movement in the last couple of years has increased the margins dramatically and made it a lot easier to get investment and funding to build a project of this scale," said Hanking Gold's chief development officer John Zimmermann.

" Our cost index for the first 10 years is well under $1,800 an ounce, so we are one of the most efficient gold projects in the country. "

John Zimmermann says the high price of gold has helped the project to attract finance. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

The operation will include surface mining of easy-to-access low-grade ore, and high-grade ore from underground workings.

The Mount Bundy Gold Project is one of more than 20 old operations being revived across Australia, in the rush to capitalise on the high price of gold.

Figures from the federal Department of Industry, Science and Resources show last financial year, gold surpassed gas, to tie with coal, as Australia's second most valuable export, after iron ore.

Visitors at the sod-turning ceremony for the construction of the mine's processing plant. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

The NT's biggest gold mine is Newmont's Granites mine in the Tanami desert north-west of Alice Springs, which has been producing since 1986, while the historic Nobles Nob mine near Tennant Creek was re-opened by Pan African Resources last year.

The Mount Bundy mine is expected to become the NT's second largest operation, and to have the largest processing plant.

Preparations under way

A 400-bed worker accommodation camp is already being built, and contractors from around the country have welcomed winning the construction work the mine is offering in the NT's otherwise flat economy.

Glen Weir says Australia's new gold rush is boosting local businesses. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Chief executive of Perth contractor CPC Engineering, Glen Weir, said winning the $30 million processing plant construction contract had been a great boost to the business.

"This project will not only be good for the construction workers, but then for all the service industries that follow on after," he said.

"There's a very good future for gold. For example, in Western Australia, there's 10 gold plants being designed and constructed in the next few years."

Hanking Gold will need to drain the old mining pit and remove all the crocodiles from it. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

To resume mining, Hanking Gold will need to drain the old Mount Bundy operation's flooded pits, and remove the crocodiles that have been found in them.

The mine is only 10 kilometres away from the densely crocodile-populated Mary River system.

The company has gained environmental approvals, and it has promised its tailings dam and wastewater will not cause pollution.

It has already built a $3 million water treatment plant on the site.

Hanking Gold has built a water treatment plant to clean the mine's wastewater. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"We've got very strict environmental conditions on our licence," Mr Zimmermann said.

"We have to keep the cyanide in the tailings averaging 20 parts per million, which is considered safe for the environment.

"We have a detoxification circuit in the tailings prior to discharge, and then any water that comes off the tailings is reclaimed and reprocessed so no cyanide in water enters the environment."

World.title: 'High-risk' youth bailed, police station vandalised in outback town
World.content:
The state's police union claims a young repeat offender in Coober Pedy was unable to be fitted with an ankle monitor while on supervised bail, and is calling for "urgent intervention" to bolster the town's policing resources.

The incident, along with an unrelated alleged attack on the local police station, has prompted the Police Association of South Australia (PASA) to write to South Australia's Deputy Premier Kyam Maher.

In the letter, sighted by the ABC, the union requested Mr Maher to "intervene as a matter of urgency" as the impact of ongoing understaffing has exposed officers and the community to "foreseeable risks".

"There is a real risk that these known and unmanaged hazards will culminate in a preventable tragedy affecting either a police officer or a member of the community," PASA president Wade Burns wrote in the letter.

The union said a youth offender who was released from detention last week had a history of offending including trespass, motor vehicle theft and breaches of bail, as well as driving stolen vehicles toward police.

Police union president Wade Burns sent a letter to Deputy Premier Kyam Maher. (ABC News)

Mr Burns wrote more recent and "serious" offending had led to the youth spending three weeks in custody, but he claimed the youth had been granted supervised bail without an ankle bracelet monitor.

"The association understands that Youth Justice is unable to implement electronic monitoring in Coober Pedy because there are no local Youth Justice staff available to fit or monitor the device," Mr Burns wrote.

"Given the youth's extensive offending history, there is a genuine concern that [they] will quickly return to criminal activity.

The ABC contacted the SA Department of Human Services, which provides youth justice services, but on Wednesday the department declined to comment about its ability to facilitate electronic monitoring in the Far North town.

Station vandalised in separate incident

Local officers also lodged a hazard report after a separate incident last Monday, involving an "intoxicated man" who allegedly vandalised the police station.

In the letter, Mr Burns said the incident happened just after 8:45pm when the man allegedly "attended the front entrance … which was closed and secured" and "used a rock to smash the front glass door".

A SA Police spokesperson confirmed a man was arrested and no officers were injured.

The interior of Coober Pedy Police Station which was vandalised. (Supplied: Police Association of South Australia)

The station served around 4,000 people but was "critically under-resourced", according to Mr Burns, with only eight of 19 positions filled.

In January, that figure was 10.

"Inadequate policing resources, limited overnight police coverage and the inability of another government agency to provide an appropriate supervision mechanism creates an obvious and foreseeable risk," Mr Burns wrote.

Do you know more about this story? Get in touch with George Yankovich at george.yankovich@proton.me

Deadlock after plan rejected

Last year, PASA lodged an ongoing South Australian Employment Tribunal (SAET) claim against SA Police to resolve the perceived issues in Coober Pedy.

PASA proposed sweeping incentives to attract officers to the remote post, including rent-free housing, on-call allowances and 45 per cent overtime loading.

SA Police rejected that plan, arguing it would add roughly $1 million to its annual budget.

SA Police say they are "committed to maintaining policing services in regional and remote communities". (ABC News: Che Chorley)

An SA Police spokesperson said it would continue monitoring resource requirements across the state and is committed to maintaining services across regional and remote communities.

"If the [SAET] recommendations were to be adopted, it would result in significant inequity across regional locations," the spokesperson said.

"It would see officers at Coober Pedy receiving remuneration equivalent to those required to live and work on the [APY] Lands or Oodnadatta and disproportionate to those at other regional locations.

"For these reasons SAPOL will not implement the non-binding recommendation."

The tribunal case is ongoing.

Coober Pedy is about 700 kilometres south of Alice Springs. (ABC News: Lee Robinson)

An SA government spokesperson, who did not directly comment on the union's letter, said it has invested more than $300 million in SA Police since 2022.

"South Australia has the highest per capita rate of frontline officers out of any Australian state and these investments are reflected in falling crime, and one of the lowest youth offender rates of any state," the spokesperson said.

For the people in Australia's opal mining capital, media reports of crime in their town was a concern.



The Coober Pedy Retail, Business & Tourism Association said while the town had "experienced several recent incidents of property crime", these had been "presented without the broader context".

"The reality is that thousands of visitors travel to Coober Pedy every year without incident," the association said in the statement.

"A town carved from rock by pioneers should not be portrayed as a community living in fear of children.

"We encourage anyone considering a visit to speak directly with local tourism operators, accommodation providers or community organisations."

World.title: Colombia survivors reflect on quake terror as rescuers search rubble
World.content:
The search for survivors from a devastating earthquake in western Colombia is growing more desperate, as rescuers enter a third day of trying to retrieve people from the wreckage.

Alejandro Eder, the mayor of Colombia's third-largest city, Cali, said rescue teams were still finding signs of people alive under the rubble and were racing to save them.

"The next 20 hours are the most critical to find and rescue people alive," he said. "Every minute is vital."

The Colombian government has declared three days of mourning for the more than 250 people known to have died.

But the disaster is testing the new government of President Abelardo de la Espriella, who was sworn in only days before the earthquake hit.

Yesterday, he said around 200 people remained missing, but a civilian-run database has put the number at more than 4,000.

Buildings have been flattened in Pereira. (Reuters: Juan David Duque)

There is concern about where swathes of displaced Colombians will go. Schools and sports arenas have been converted to temporary shelters in the worst-hit regions.

In Pereira, the hard-hit city in the foothills of the Andes, Juliana Maya stood in front of the rubble that was once her bakery, Las Delicias de Mauro.

The building housing Juliana Maya's bakery and her family home collapsed during the quake. (ABC News)

When the earthquake hit, she and more than a dozen co-workers were inside.

"It started to shake back and forth. We immediately went outside, and everything around the bakery started to fall," she said.

"At one point the entire bakery collapsed, too."

Her family's home was part of the same building.

"I have my mother-in-law, who is elderly, and my father-in-law, who is hospitalised," she said.

"They have absolutely nothing … they are elderly and we don't have a place to put them."

Comprehending a new reality

Walter Arroyave was in his apartment in Pereira when the earthquake struck.

His wife and daughter had already left for work and school, so he was alone.

About 1,600 buildings were reported damaged or collapsed after the quake. (Reuters: Luisa Gonzalez)

"First, I took cover in the doorway of the apartment," he said.

"But then, I don't know — anxiety, or — I don't know… it led me to go down and leave the apartment."

Mr Arroyave said he had never experienced anything so frightening and horrible.

"I went to my mum and dad's house. I checked that they were OK, but then when I tried to reach my wife, she wouldn't answer, wouldn't answer, wouldn't answer. I started to panic terribly."

The roads were choked with motorcycles and cars, and power outages had cut the traffic lights.

It took two and a half hours for him to hear through others that his wife was safe and had been to his daughter's school.

Teams of people have been working to clear piles of debris. (Reuters: Juan David Duque)

Now he is trying to comprehend his city's new reality.

"You see earthquake news, but you never imagine that it's going to happen to you, to your family, to people you know," he said.

'Receiving care in a hallway'

Further south in Cali, a city of 2 million people, numerous buildings have been flattened.

People have formed human chains, passing chunks of concrete and wreckage, to help clear the sites of collapsed buildings.

Bogotá fire department official Camilo Cano, who is in Cali, said more than 48 hours later, the rescue efforts were focusing on the removal of debris.

"And we are still continuing to try to find victims alive at this moment," he said.

"We still have hope until at least four days after the earthquake have passed."

Teams in Cali are still working to remove rubble and debris. (AP: Juan Diaz)

Cali resident Abraham Gutierrez had admitted his mother to a hospital clinic the day before the earthquake.

She has mobility issues stemming from cancer.

After the earthquake, he spent several distressing hours trying to find out if she was still alive.

But now he is not sure how she will continue to receive her medical care, with health facilities completely overwhelmed and the city's largest public hospital sustaining considerable damage.

"They had to evacuate her … she is receiving care in a hallway, because there are no emergency rooms actually available," Mr Gutierrez said.

"There is no real emergency care available in the main hospitals."

Aid groups pivot

Pereira is part of Colombia's "Coffee Axis", a UNESCO World Heritage site known for its traditional industry and unique architecture.

The earthquake has impacted other cities including Quibdó, Manizales and Armenia, and disrupted roads, transportation and telecommunications.

Volunteers sorted aid for people affected by the quake. (AP: Santiago Saldarriaga)

Some aid groups were already present in the coffee-growing region to support a 2016 peace accord between the Colombian government and leftist guerilla rebels.

Conflicts between other armed groups in the region have persisted, particularly in the Choco area, which was badly hit by the earthquake.

Now those aid groups are pivoting to disaster relief.

There is also assistance flowing in from other nations around the region.

The US has announced $US15.5 million ($21.9 million) in aid and is sending State Department humanitarian experts to the country.

Mexico, Brazil and Ecuador have also offered help.

How the US is running Venezuela Amid the fallout of devastating twin earthquakes Donald Trump says the US has been taking "billions and billions of dollars from Venezuela". So what is happening with the seized funds?

El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele said his country was sending 100 tonnes of supplies on two cargo planes.

Mr Bukele said in a post on X that the Colombian government had requested assistance solely in the form of supplies.

"We have been informed that their rescue teams, medical personnel, and other emergency response units are deployed and addressing the situation, so at this time, they do not require support in the form of personnel," he wrote.

"May God bless and protect Colombia."

ABC/wires

World.title: More judges and incentives for early guilty pleas proposed to fix case backlog
World.content:
An independent review into Tasmania's court backlog has recommended 20 changes that could improve how quickly matters are dealt with and free up court resources.

The Third Party Review of Backlogs in the Tasmanian Court System, written by Lloyd Babb, proposed moving matters that are better dealt with by a tribunal or an infringement notice out of the Magistrates Court, and legislating a sentence-reduction scheme for early guilty pleas.

Other recommendations include improving evidence disclosure between legal parties, involving legal aid in the early resolution of committal matters, and moving all residential tenancy disputes to the Tasmanian Civil and Administrative Tribunal.

"I also recommend implementing an initial 'super call-over' process that can help to 'clear the decks' by getting as many matters as possible appropriately finalised," Mr Babb wrote.

Better training for frontline officers and police prosecutors on evidence disclosure and legislating mandatory, committal-stage conferences between the defence and the prosecution were also recommended.

The review was a recommendation from Tasmania's justice system leaders following the Justice Forum in Hobart last year.

The Tasmanian government has accepted in full or in principle 19 of the 20 recommendations, with one requiring further consideration.

Mr Babb also suggested Tasmania increase the number of Supreme Court judges and have a pool of reserve judges.

Backlog a growing problem with no single solution

If you had the chance to sentence a criminal, how hard would you go? How would you sentence this "armed robber"? Would you lock her up, or after hearing her personal story, would you be more lenient?

The Supreme Court Annual Report 2024-2025 shows 912 criminal non-appeal cases pending as of June 30 last year, a 139 per cent increase from a decade ago.

"Conducting a review process such as this is an excellent reminder that perfect systems and perfect solutions do not exist," Mr Babb said.

"Tasmania's current criminal justice process habitually pushes out the timeframes for resolutions in criminal matters, often causing cases to remain in the system far longer than they need to.

"This contributes significantly to creating unsustainable delays and backlogs.

" Having been the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) in both Australia's largest and smallest jurisdictions, I have a direct understanding of the different challenges faced by each. "

Mr Babb said the recommendations were not the only possible way to tackle the issue of backlogs, but will likely lead to meaningful improvements.

"Tasmania should structurally discourage slow, late-stage matter finalisations and strategically position policy, effort and resources to prompt consistent, good quality, early-stage finalisations," he said.

"Compared to the Australian average, the Tasmanian Supreme Court uses fewer full-time equivalent judges to finalise matters.

" Nevertheless, Tasmania consistently experiences higher percentages of delayed finalisations of criminal cases than other states and territories. "

Attorney-General and Minister for Justice Guy Barnett said Tasmanians should have access to a justice system that is efficient, effective and responsive.

"Mr Babb has produced a comprehensive expert report to government … I thank him for his significant contribution, expertise and engagement with stakeholders across Tasmania's justice system," Mr Barnett said.

"The recommendations will help inform the next phase of work to strengthen Tasmania's justice system and deliver more timely outcomes for court users.

World.title: Storm Boy made Mr Percival famous. Now pelicans like him are under threat
World.content:
As he travels down the waters of Coorong, past sand dunes where scenes from the first Storm Boy movie were filmed more than 50 years ago, Dr Greg Johnston is clear about what must be done to help pelicans and other bird species survive the oncoming bird flu.

"We need to look after the animals' habitat so they have maximum chance of recovering," he says.

Dr Greg Johnston has been tracking South Australia's pelicans for decades. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

Everything you need to know about Australia's bird flu surge There are more than 200 confirmed cases of the deadly H5N1 bird flu strain across Australia. Here's how it spreads and what to know.

As an adjunct associate professor with Flinders University who has been tracking South Australia's pelicans for 37 years, Johnston is realistic about what the advancing spread of H5N1 bird flu will likely mean for them, as well as the other hundreds of bird species found in the Coorong.

The Coorong is an important breeding sanctuary for Australian pelicans, with thousands of the birds calling the region home.

Like most scientists, Johnston has been expecting bird flu's arrival for some years, watching it spread from wild birds to domestic poultry in 2020 in central Asia, then through Europe, Africa and North and South America.

Pelicans can live up to 25 years in the wild, and longer in captivity. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

While he says the predicting effect the disease will have on Australian pelicans still involves some "guesswork", data from overseas suggests those in breeding colonies such as the Coorong or Bird Island, off the coast of metropolitan Adelaide, could lose between 60 and 70 per cent of their population in the first wave of the virus.

Coorong's pelicans were brought to prominence in the book Storm Boy and its film adaptions. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

Johnston says pelicans, like other birds and mammals, are likely in for a "fairly torrid" two or three years as the virus spreads and recurs.

"Viruses evolve like other organisms do," he says, pointing to the European black-headed gull, which he describes as equivalent to the silver gull in Australia.

The black-headed gull was largely unaffected by the initial arrival of the disease in Europe, but in the outbreak's second year its population was "badly hit".

Pelicans, however, were very badly affected during the initial spread of the disease — and then were "hit even harder" in the second year.

"Most species are going to have survivors — as long as they have safe spaces to do that," he says.

Greater crested terns are seen in abundance at the Goolwa Barrage and into the Coorong. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

The decline of bird numbers in the Coorong has been well documented over the years.

In the 1980s, it supported 250,000 migrating red neck stints over the summer season.

That number had already dropped to 25,000 by 2010, a measure of the reduction of the Coorong's ability to support wildlife.

Although pelicans are not considered endangered, Johnston says aerial censuses showed their numbers in Australia's south-east have been declining by 1 per cent per year for 40 years due to natural swamp lands drying up and more water diverted for human usage.

Pelicans at the mouth of the Murray River, with pipes from the dredging work that is necessary to keep the mouth of the river open. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

The Murray-Darling Basin Plan is currently under review, and the report is due to be delivered to the government in December.

Locals are waiting to see what this could mean for this fragile environment at the very end of the river system.

Coorong a 'magical' bird sanctuary

Skipper Joel Hirsch takes tourists out to the Coorong several times a week. They pass the Murray Mouth and the dredger, its black pipe now a sought-after resting place for dozens of snoozing long-nosed seals.

The dredger works to keep the mouth of the 2,500-kilometre-long Murray River from closing over, and has done so for the majority of the time since 2002.

Hirsch's tours point out many of the places in which scenes from both versions of the movie Storm Boy were filmed, and he considers the pelican to be an iconic part of his home region.

One of the historic shacks that has survived within the Coorong National Park. (ABC South East: Caroline Horn)

"Everything about the Coorong is absolutely magical," he says.

"Anything that's going on in the environment — so whether it's low water, water releases, algal blooms, bird flu — we always discuss everything that's going on, and try to give a bit of perspective [on] the environment and the challenges that exist," Hirsch says.

Greg Rowe as Mike, a young boy whose friendship with a pelican named Mr Percival forms the emotional heart of Storm Boy. (Supplied: NFSA)

The original film adaption of Storm Boy was shot in and around Goolwa and the Coorong in the 1970s, with the 50th anniversary of its release being celebrated this year.

The pelican that starred as Mr Percival lived a "low-key" life at Adelaide Zoo for many years after filming, before passing away at the age of 33 in 2009.

Pelicans live for about 25 years in the wild. (ABC South East: Caroline Horn)

Totem connection

Mark Koolmatrie is a Tanganekald elder from the Ngarrindjeri Nation.

He runs cultural tours in several areas, including the Coorong, and says the nori (Australian pelican), kungari (black swan) and waatji pulyeri (blue fairy-wrens), along with other animals and plants, are Ngartji (totems) connecting people to ruwe (Country).

Ngarrindjeri elder Mark Koolmatrie is visited by a throkeri (silver gull) while being interviewed about bird flu. The throkeri was his mother's Ngartji (totem). (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

"It's our identity of who we are as South Australians, and who we are as Ngarrindjeri people, and what the Kurangk (Coorong) means," he said.

"Some people have the nori as their totem. And so when the nori is sick, so are they.

"It is a mental anguish that is put on them as well."

Like Johnston and Hirsch, he wants the government, as it reviews the Murray-Darling Basin Plan, to understand the need to support the fragile environment of the Coorong and the bird life it will support through the trying times ahead.

"With the dredge being there, it demonstrates that there is not enough water that's coming through," he said.

Pelicans in the north lagoon of the Coorong in 2025. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

Mr Koolmatrie is urging all Australians to visit the Coorong at least once in their lifetime.

"Come and have a look at the wildlife, the birds that are around the place. Please come and have a look at them and give them your support," he says.

"Let them know like, 'Hey, we're here for you.'"

If you see a sick or dead bird: Do not touch it.

Take note of the location and, if possible, take photos.

Report it to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline: 1800 675 888.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Thousands of students expected to walk out of class in protest of One Nation; White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt to step down
World.content:
Thousands of students are expected to walk out of class today in protest of Pauline Hanson’s One Nation.

The nationwide “students say no to Hanson” protest, with events in state and territory capitals, is hoping to attract thousands of students angry at the ascendent party’s policies, particularly on changes to the school curriculum regarding Australian history and gender.

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce, with party leader Pauline Hanson. Alex Ellinghausen

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce accused “socialist” school teachers of encouraging students to participate in protests against his party on Thursday, as Education Minister Jason Clare cautions children to stay in class and move their protest to the weekend.

“[Students have] been told to hate this country, and they’ve been advised by people – because it’s not on the students’ own volition – they’ve been advised by a clique of people who have a political purpose,” Joyce said on Wednesday.

World.title: ‘Once in a lifetime’: Millions gather in Europe to see first total solar eclipse in decades
World.content:
WorldEuropeSpace ‘Once in a lifetime’: Millions gather in Europe to see first total solar eclipse in decades Corina Pons and Tom Little August 13, 2026 — 6:21am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Madrid/Reykjavik: The skies above Iceland fell into total darkness as a full solar eclipse occurred over the country’s westernmost coast, as a break in the clouds allowed holidaymakers and locals to glimpse the celestial phenomenon. Live footage from Reykjavik showed on Wednesday (Iceland time) that, despite the overcast sky, a cheer went up from the crowd gathered in front of Hallgrimskirkja church when everything went black above them. The total solar eclipse is seen in Palencia, Spain. Getty Images Millions of people gathered in Iceland and northern Spain to witness Western Europe’s first total solar eclipse in 27 years, with Spanish officials warning people to avoid areas where a heatwave has raised the risk of wildfires. Authorities were expecting up to 6 million visitors in mostly rural areas within the eclipse’s path across the north of Spain and the Balearic Islands, said Juan Cruz, Spain’s Secretary of State for Science.



“I hope that tonight will see the emergence of a wonderful generation of astrophysicists,” he said. “It’s such a special moment.” The eclipse was quickly followed by the sunset in Spain, making the event particularly alluring. The uncanny sensation when day briefly turns into twilight and some animals fall quiet as the moon passes directly between Earth and the sun, was often treated as an omen in the past, a cosmic struggle or a sign of divine power.



Now, Spain sees it as a chance to showcase seldom-visited regions and draw tourists away from its overcrowded beach resorts, while also rolling out a massive police operation and public safety campaign to prevent them from causing wildfires. Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told reporters that 25,000 police officers had been assigned to guarantee security around the eclipse observation while nearly 100 planes and helicopters were also being deployed. People observing a partial eclipse at Northala Fields in London. AP Photo/Frank Augstein A man watches with a welding shield in Herten, Germany. AP Photo/Martin Meissner Lola Guerreiro spent the night in the mountains near Arcos de las Salinas in eastern Spain, home to Galactica – Europe’s largest educational astronomy centre – as well as the Javalambre observatory, after making the long drive from Extremadura to view the eclipse.



“Watching a total solar eclipse has been a dream of mine for many, many years, and I didn’t want to miss the chance to experience it, even though it meant a seven-hour journey,” she said. Sergio, a 60-year-old Italian, had made the trek in a camping van with his family to Arija in northern Spain. The eclipse seen at El Monte De San Pedro park in Spain. Getty Images People cast long shadows while watching from the top of a mine dump in Gremany. AP Photo/Martin Meissner “I do feel a little emotional. Yes, because I know I won’t have another chance in my life to see an eclipse, a phenomenon like this,” he said.



The Iberian Peninsula last saw a total solar eclipse in 1912. It is set to experience another one on August 2, 2027, and an annular eclipse in January 2028, completing the so-called “Iberian Eclipse Trio”. In Iceland’s capital Reykjavik, glasses to allow people to look at the phenomenon without damaging their eyes have been sold out for days as the Nordic country of roughly 400,000 people expects to welcome up to 80,000 visitors. The eclipse seen form Palencia, Spain. Millions gathered across the country to witness the event. Getty Images People observe the partial eclipse with special protective glasses in Liverpool, England. AP Photo/Jon Super Totality – when the moon completely covers the sun’s light – reached Iceland’s westernmost coast at about 5:44 pm local time (3.44am on Thursday, AEST). It cast the far west of the island nation into total darkness for more than two minutes, though most cities saw shorter periods of darkness. The moon’s shadow then continued its trajectory eastwards.



Authorities had warned of heavy traffic and urged viewers to arrive early. Singer Björk was due to perform a DJ set at an eclipse-themed event south of Reykjavik. US space agency NASA plans to fly a high-altitude WB-57 aircraft from Iceland to follow the moon’s shadow, and NASA-funded teams will launch balloons to study how the sudden darkness and cooling affect the lower atmosphere. A beachgoer wearing special eclipse glasses looks up from Puerto de Sagunto beach near Valencia, Spain. AP Photo/Alberto Saiz The moon and the sun set in the Gulf of Finland, seen from St. Petersburg, Russia. AP Photo/Dmitri Lovetsky Aside from casual observers, the event also draws “eclipse chasers”, enthusiasts who crisscross the globe to be in the path of totality whenever an eclipse occurs.



Gordon Telepun, a retired plastic surgeon and amateur astronomer from the U.S. who has photographed six total eclipses, said he would watch from the island of Mallorca because Spain checked all the boxes for eclipse chasers.
