These kinds of scams are sometimes referred to as “pig butchering” operations, a term that originated with romance scams and graphically evokes the process of fattening up a prospective victim with flattery before draining them financially. Most of the emails don’t mention money, instead they lead with flattery. Like romance scams, author scams target vulnerability and play on emotions. “They’re trying to capitalise on an author’s genuine desire to have their work published, to have their work promoted, to have their work adapted,” Hayward says. The tactic has proved remarkably lucrative for its perpetrators. In a recent case, the US government determined that just one of these publishing scam operations, based in the Philippines, defrauded nearly 800 writers of more than $48 million over six years. US author Victoria Strauss, who has covered author scams since 1998 via the website Writer Beware, says they have proliferated over the past decade, fuelled by outfits based in the Philippines, Pakistan and India. The more recent AI-driven scams come from a different location, however.



“I’ve gotten hundreds of reports of these AI scams, and I traced a lot of them back to the payment information, and everything that I can collect and deduce indicates that they primarily come from Nigeria,” says Strauss. “I see them as kind of a descendant of the ‘Nigerian prince’ scams of old.” Authors who have been inundated with these kinds of emails have become far more adept at identifying them. “The AI-generated copy is its own genre now and you can spot it once you’ve seen a few,” says Gardiner. The emails also have telling similarities: “same terms, same logic, same sentence structures”. Lucy Hayward, the chief executive of the Australian Society of Authors. They’re also often about older books. Gardiner says most of the scam emails she receives “are about two young adult books I published years ago. Perhaps it’s something to do with how often they were ingested in a pirate database used to train AI. No real publicist would want to talk to me about them, although sometimes local schools or readers do, so I always have to check.” Hayward says sifting the real emails from the fake has become a problem in itself. “[At this point] it’s not so much that authors are falling for these scams and handing out money, it’s the volume of the emails that they are receiving. It becomes very difficult to determine what might be a legitimate offer and what is a scam.” One of the key ways to check is looking at the email address, she says, “but for Australia, we have a smaller market, and where book clubs and podcasts are concerned, you might not have someone with a professional email address”. They’re trying to capitalise on an author’s genuine desire to have their work published, to have their work promoted, to have their work adapted. “You waste time trying to sift the real from the fake,” Gardiner says. “No doubt some genuine approaches have not got through, too, which means writers and readers miss out on real opportunities to engage.”



How are scammers continuing to thrive, if authors are getting wise? Strauss says the dozen or so emails she receives each week about people who have lost money to these scams involve non-professional and first-time authors. “There are a lot of people who just want to write one book; they want to write a memoir, or they want to write about their cancer journey or something they feel is meaningful and will help people. There are a lot of older people who retire and write children’s stories, or a memoir,” she says. Related Article Literature The Australian author who went from rejection letters to global bestseller These people are vulnerable to scammers in more than one way: not only are they unaware of how the publishing industry works and outside professional support networks and communities, but the personal nature of their material can make them particularly susceptible to emotional manipulation. “I sometimes hear from the relatives of older people, often on fixed incomes, who’ve lost enormous amounts of money – tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars – and cannot be convinced that they’re being scammed because the scammers are using psychological manipulation to establish personal relationships,” Strauss says. As she embarks on her career, Colussi can well understand how people are taken in. “Writing a book is such a dream for so many people. They are waiting for that one ‘yes’, and pretending that you are that one ‘yes’ is unfortunately an easy way to take advantage of someone.” What else is happening in the book world?

World.title: 'Huge demand on services': North Shore ambulance patients diverted to Whāngarei
World.content:
Wellsford GP on Auckland ambulance patients sent to Whangarei Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Some Auckland ambulance patients are being taken to Whāngarei Hospital because North Shore Hospital is too full to take them.

That is despite the much smaller Whāngarei Hospital already struggling with extremely high patient numbers this winter.

RNZ understands diversions were taking place on Tuesday night which was also very busy at Whāngarei's emergency department.

Diversions were happening also last week.

Tim Malloy is a GP for Coast to Coast healthcare group which has a clinic in Auckland's most northern town Wellsford, just shy of the Northland border.

He was sent a letter by St John Ambulance last week telling him any patients from the northern part of the Rodney district who needed to go to an ED would be taken to Whāngarei. They were normally serviced by North Shore.

That was "due to the huge demand on the services at North Shore Hospital", he said.

RNZ understands Whāngarei was already under serious pressure itself. It is about half the size of North Shore.

Health NZ director of operations Brad Healy said it was a "very small number" of ambulances that were actually diverted to Whangarei.

"This practice is not unusual and used at times to manage demand and ensure patients can receive care as quickly as possible. In some instances, depending on the location of the patient, Whangārei Hospital is closer in travel time than North Shore Hospital," he said.

Malloy said the letter was the first his practice had ever received about the ambulance diversions.

Busy winter in northern Auckland

This winter was the busiest Malloy had seen in 37 years as a GP.

Patients in Coast to Coast's urgent care clinic were sometimes waiting five hours and staff have had to be brought in on their days off to help, he said

"When you have 15 people waiting for you and you have a serious illness you are trying to manage in a patient while you wait for an ambulance to arrive, and all these patients are just having to wait, it's incredibly stressful. For all of us," he said.

Most of the patients coming into urgent care had respiratory infections. The cases seemed to last longer - and there were a growing number of secondary infections, he said.

There were very high numbers of people with influenza and it was "hammering all our communities".

It was proving to be a particularly severe winter with patients sicker for longer and illnesses were affecting not just the vulnerable but also normally healthy people.

He told Morning Report patients were grateful to get any help so it was "slightly academic" to them whether their ambulance headed north or south.

Malloy wanted to see a campaign to encourage people to get vaccinated against flu - and for those vaccinations to be free.

It would help people stay healthy, in particular to avoid serious complications.

That would help the whole health system, he said.

World.title: Live: What's next for Christopher Luxon? Chris Penk sacked after failed National leadership challenge
World.content:
RNZ national

Chris Bishop is due to speak to media at an event after a political commentator named him as one of the senior ministers involved in a leadership challenge. Watch the livestream below.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has survived a confidence vote - the second in just four months.

On Wednesday afternoon, Luxon confirmed speculation that MP Chris Penk had challenged him for the leadership - this is despite his earlier denial.

At a press conference after an urgent Caucus meeting, Luxon said it was united and determined to win the election.

"Our focus is on National's positive plan to fix the basics and to build the future, so that we realise the incredible potential that sits in this country, and that we set it up for our kids and our grandkids."

Luxon was flanked by senior MPs, including Nicola Willis, Mark Mitchell and Chris Bishop. Standing just behind them was Erica Stanford, who was rumoured to be gunning for the top job.

With Penk's failed challenge, Luxon said his position was now untenable and he was sacked from his ministerial portfolios. Penk later said he will not stand for re-election in November.

Speaking to Morning Report on Thursday morning, political commentator Janet Wilson said there were other senior ministers involved at the Bishop was "somewhere in there trying to manoeuvre".

"When you get that kind of manoeuvring, it's deeply decisive."

Fellow commentator Liam Hehir agreed, saying Penk was made to be the "scapegoat" and what happened was inevitable.

World.title: Polling booths open in Cook Islands
World.content:
Polling is open in the Cook Islands where 11,000 registered voters will elect their leaders for the next four years.

Voting stations open at 9am on Wednesday morning, Cook Islands time (7am Thursday NZT) and will close at 6pm.

There are 24 constituencies, 10 on the main island of Rarotonga, and the other 14 spread across the Pa Enua, or outer islands.

Thirteen seats are needed for a majority to form a government.

A total of 63 candidates were confirmed for the 2026 general election, down from the 71 who contested the 2022 election. This year's lineup includes 49 men and 14 women.

With independents making up 20 per cent of candidates, should no party claim the 13 seats needed for majority, the independents could hold the power over who forms government.

One seat has already been won this election, with Mangaia's Ivirua candidate Agnes Helen Armstrong running uncontested as an independent.

There's been a delay in the Northern Cooks, as bad weather meant electoral officers were unable to get ashore in Nassau.

Officials have announced the island's polling will be postponed to Thursday afternoon local time.

The issues for voters

The local newspaper, Cook Islands News, ran a poll which found a majority - 50.5 percent - of respondents across the Pa Enua and Rarotonga identified the cost of living and inflation - including fuel prices, water and power bills, housing, transportation and consumer goods - as their primary concern.

Editor Rashneel Kumar told Pacific Waves last week that global conflicts, contributing to resource restraints and costs, have a flow-on effect on local customers.

"With the Middle East conflict, obviously, we have seen a impact on small island nations, and Cook Islands is not spared as well," he said.

"We end up the supply chain, so we do absorb a lot of additional cost - and by the time the goods land here, the prices does have an impact as well as price of energy through the increase of petrol has affected the people.

"So cost of living obviously is number one issue."

Water tariffs, seabed minerals and foreign relationships have also been heavily debated topics of interest.

World.title: Why taking risks in business may be best in uncertain times
World.content:
Taking risks could be the best course of action for businesses amid ongoing uncertainty economic and geopolitical conditions.

"The real risk is not making the wrong move in uncertain conditions. It is standing still while the environment, and your competitors, keep moving," BDO risk advisory national leader Tarunesh Singh said, reflecting on the release of the BDO Global Risk Landscape Report survey of 500 business leaders around the world.

Singh said risk and disruption was no longer the exception for businesses.

He said a New Zealand version of the report suggests that New Zealand's world view was little different from what was seen elsewhere, though local businesses were increasingly prepared to take risks.

"The culture around risk in New Zealand is shifting, and I think that the proportion of business owners and corporations that are more willing to take risk and more willing to to take action is definitely increasing year on year," Singh said.

"I think that businesses are making decisions and taking action, certainly more so than they did three or five years ago."

Singh said there was no longer a perfect time to act on investment or other critical business decisions.

He said waiting for certainty could mean waiting indefinitely, which could be costly.

"The cost of delay can be easy to underestimate. While one business holds off, others are adapting, investing and accelerating."

Among the potential cost risks were fuel price surges, shipping and logistics disruption, border settings that affect immigration and access to talent, inflation and price volatility, cost-of-living pressure and political instability, at home and abroad, all paint the same picture.

Global risk factors

The global findings point to a business environment where crisis response is becoming routine, but proactive risk management is becoming harder to sustain.

Four out of five business leaders (80 percent) say the global risk landscape was more defined by crisis than ever before with

68 seeing the speed at which crises were impacting their organisation was increasing (up 14 percent).

Geopolitical instability was also intensifying other risks, while fraud remained underestimated and many organisations continued to respond reactively rather than taking a more proactive approach to risk management.

Singh said the best way to deal with risk was to be seen to be managing it, as most cases of fraud were inside jobs by people with day-to-day access and visibility on what happens.

"It's either people internal to the organisation or close external stakeholders like suppliers seeing an opportunity over time. Then seeing that actually nobody might be watching a particular area or aspect, and then taking the opportunity that they've identified

World.title: Three big NZ petrol companies barely shift greenhouse gas emissions in a year
World.content:
Three petrol companies account for more than half of New Zealand's climate pollution - not including agriculture.

Z Energy, BP and Mobil's combined greenhouse gas emissions have barely shifted since last year, even though this year's data included the beginning of the fuel crisis sparked by conflict in the Middle East.

Overall, companies reported 31.6 million tonnes of carbon-equivalent emissions - a decrease of just under 1 million tonnes (3 percent).

The three petrol companies accounted for 16.2m tonnes of that.

Fossil fuel producers and steel and aluminium companies rounded out the top 10, with little change from last year.

The data, which is published annually by the Environmental Protection Authority, covers the year to 30 June 2026, and includes companies that are part of the Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS).

The EPA data notably excludes some of New Zealand's largest emitters, including Fonterra, after the government ended reporting requirements for agriculture in 2024.

As a result, it now accounts for less than half of the country's actual emissions, which the New Zealand Greenhouse Gas Inventory measured at 75.8m tonnes in 2024.

Despite that, it remains the only public information available where many companies' emissions can be directly compared.

Since agriculture was excluded, Z Energy has topped the list for the last two years, reporting emissions of 7.2m tonnes in the most recent year, a drop of five percent.

Its most recent corporate climate statement shows the company's overall emissions are significantly higher than what it has to report to the EPA, with 12m tonnes recorded in the 2025 calendar year.

Z has managed to halve its operational emissions - what it emits in the course of running its business - since 2019, with most of that change happening in 2022 and 2023.

However, the carbon dioxide from the fuel it sells, which accounts for the vast majority of its emissions - has stayed static.

Data no longer includes country's top emitter

Prior to last year, agriculture companies regularly made the top 10 emitters, with Fonterra topping the list every year with reported emissions that were nearly double the next-largest emitter.

The company still voluntarily discloses its greenhouse gas emissions, and a spokesperson said its latest data would included in the company's annual report next month.

Its most recent annual report showed the company emitted 26.7 million tonnes in carbon-equivalent emissions in 2025 - a 2.2 percent increase on 2024.

Most of that increase came from dairy cows, whose methane emissions account for more than three-quarters of the company's overall emissions.

Fonterra has managed to lower its on-farm emissions by about 7 percent since 2018, which it uses as a baseline reporting year.

The company still reports a small proportion of its emissions to the EPA, from the coal it uses in its industrial processes.

Those emissions alone were still high enough to earn it a 13th placing out of nearly 130 companies on the list.

Other companies previously in the top 10 who no longer have to report their emissions include meat processors Affco and Alliance, milk exporter Open Country Dairy, and Silver Fern Farms - which also voluntarily discloses its emissions.

Its latest disclosure, for 2025, showed 4.8m tonnes of emissions - most of that also from methane produced by livestock.

Genesis was the sole energy company to feature in the top 10, almost entirely due to its ownership of the coal-fired Huntly power station.

Its emissions dropped dramatically from 2024-25, though.

In a statement, the company said that was consistent with a 42 percent decrease in the amount of coal the company had to burn last winter, compared to 2024 when low hydro levels and a gas shortage combined to create a winter energy crisis.

Genesis was investing in renewable energy and battery storage, but Huntly still played a critical role for now, the statement said.

"As a result, annual emissions are expected to fluctuate, while the long-term trend continues downward."

Other gentailers were able to draw on Huntly as back-up generation - but Genesis still carried the emissions.

More than 70 percent of the company's light commercial and passenger vehicles was now electric or hybrid and the company planned to convert to a fully electric fleet by 2028, it said.

World.title: Thousands sell houses for less than they paid
World.content:
Just over 13 percent of all properties sold in the second quarter of this year changed hands for less than the seller paid for them, and the number tops 20 percent in Auckland.

Cotality has released its latest "pain and gain" report, which tracks how many sellers are taking a loss. It will understate the true number because it does not include the costs of sale, such as real estate agent commissions.

Across the country 13.1 percent of properties sold in the second quarter were at a loss, the highest number since 2012. In Auckland, the proportion was 20.9 percent and in Wellington it was 18.4 percent.

Why have Ooshies taken over my house? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

The median amount lost was $60,000, for a total loss of $159 million. The median gross profit was $280,000, down from $440,000 at the peak.

People who made money on their properties had held them for a record length of time - 10.4 years. People who sold had only held for a median 4.3 years.

Cotality chief economist Kelvin Davidson said that could indicate that people were choosing to hold for longer than previously to wait for a market recovery or because selling was more difficult than usual.

Apartments were much more likely to be sold for a loss, at 45.4 percent.

It was the weakest resale performance for apartments since 2010.

Davidson said apartments had fallen in value by 6 percent on average in the past 12 months compared to 2 percent for townhouses and little movement for standalone swellings.

He said apartments tend to be more likely to resell at a loss because they did not have as much capital growth over time, even in an upswing. "They're a bit more vulnerable to being sold at a loss simply because they haven't made as much capital gain through the cycle so that's part of it."

Some parts of the country had very small percentages selling for a loss such as Timaru and Gore, where 1.8 percent of sales lost money.

Davidson said the pattern was consistent with lower house prices.

"It's been a pretty sluggish housing market for a number of years so no surprise that resellers are not faring as well as they have done in the past. The 13 percent of resales in the second quarter sold for a loss is the highest figure we've seen for 11 or 12 years but it's been more of a slow grind downwards, it hasn't been the sharp adjustment we saw in the global financial crisis.

"Back then, the share of properties being sold for a loss rose from nothing to about 20 percent in a year or two. This time it's risen from nothing to around 13 percent in four or five years so it's been an adjustment but it's been a bit slower than what we've seen in the past. It's consistent with the servicing testing that we've got within the banks now.

"People who might have run into problems and had to sell sooner than what they thought, perhaps haven't even got the mortgage in the first place. And also employment has stayed up, people have stayed in work. So that's helped sellers in terms of they can hold on a little bit longer if they need to. They don't necessarily have to sell at a loss."

He said the four-year median hold period for losses went back to the start of the housing market slowdown.

"We've seen regionally Auckland's still a little bit weaker, Wellington's a little bit weaker. There's perhaps no great surprises there."

He said he did not expect things to turn around any time soon.

"We've still got economic uncertainty. If anything, mortgage rates are sneaking higher. There are still a lot of listings out there. It's a buyer's market. So I just think house prices might not necessarily fall too much further because affordability has been restored quite a lot, but they may not necessarily rise any time soon either. And with that pricing power probably resting with buyers, it's going to be just a little bit challenging for sellers or property resellers for the next little while."

World.title: The housing market stand-off
World.content:
New Zealand's property market is stuck in a stand-off, as buyers take their time over their purchases while vendors are unwilling to move on price, the Real Estate Institute says.

Its latest data shows prices were steady in July. The national median price of $760,000 was down 0.7 percent compared to July 2025. The house price index, which smoothes out fluctuations caused by the type of properties selling, was down 0.4 percent. Excluding Auckland, the index was up 0.2 percent.

But the number of properties sold was down 10 percent to 6090. Auckland's turnover was down 8.9 percent.

There were 7698 new listings and the "days to sell" measure, which represents the length of time it would take to clear the available stock at the current rate of sale, was up two days to 50.

Why have Ooshies taken over my house? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

The institute said it was the fifth-slowest July on record.

The picture was mixed around the country, though. Otago's house price index hit an all-time high and Canterbury had the fourth-busiest July since the institute's records began.

Chief executive Lizzy Ryley said the official cash rate increase, cost of living pressure, global uncertainty and the approaching election were all factors.

New Zealand's prices are still down 17 percent from the peak, while Auckland's are down 25 percent and Wellington's just over 29 percent.

Compared to last year, Auckland's prices are down 1.7 percent and Wellington's 4.4 percent but Canterbury's are up 4 percent and Otago's almost 5 percent.

Real Estate Institute chief corporate affairs officer Trey Sarten said the drop in activity was noticeable.

"It's interesting because it's a bit of an infinite loop because the buyers having more time and choice leads to longer time on market, so the inventory starts to build up and the vendors are not blinking on price, and so there is a bit of a stand-off of who's going to blink first.

"I think generally there is uncertainty across the board, and so whether it's with New Zealand as a country or globally with events around the world happening, whether that's political or natural events, there is uncertainty that is preventing people from making a decision, so buyers are continuing to be cautious and sellers are holding out for that right offer to come along."

He said the steadiness in the market was likely to continue while uncertainty was high.

"But it's certainly not one national story as regions continue to operate on different speeds."

World.title: The plan to strengthen Auckland's gateway for cruise industry
World.content:
Auckland Council plan to bring more cruise ships to city Morning Report Download MP3 5m

An ambitious plan to strengthen Auckland's role as the gateway for the cruise industry is expected to result in smoother sailing for the rest of the country.

"When Auckland performs well, the cruise system across Aotearoa benefits," a report by Auckland Council's economic and cultural agency Tātaki Auckland Unlimited (TAU) said.

"Although the city accounts for only 15 percent of nationwide (cruise) passenger movements - totalling 236,240 passengers and 103,030 crew in the 2023/24 season - it generates a disproportionately high share of economic value.

The Auckland region's cruise business generated around $244.6 million in gross domestic product and supported about 3780 jobs in the 2023/24 season.

However, a downturn over the past couple of years saw the industry shrink, along with its contribution to jobs and the economy, and the knock-on benefits for the rest of New Zealand tourism industry.

Cruise ship industry in the doldrums

The Cruise Association raised the alarm a couple of years ago, following the launch of a national strategy in August 2024.

But it had been tough going ever since.

By November 2024, the industry's plan was moving in the opposite direction, amid rising costs, industry disorganisation and a sharp 20 percent drop on bookings for 2024/25 on the year earlier.

The number dropped again in 2025/26 by 40 percent on the peak 2023/24 season with an uncertain outlook for the upcoming season.

"Despite strong appeal and ratings, New Zealand faces forecast softness in 2026/27 driven by macro factors (fuel, FX, geopolitics) and local cost/regulatory settings-reinforcing the need for destination competitiveness and clarity of value," TAU's report said.

Still, IDNZ managing director Debbie Summers who specialises in all manner of cruise passenger logistics on the ground, said developing Auckland's gateway was key to the industry's overall success.

"Cruise tourism is right now bringing in over $1 billion overall in economic spend for the country. That's without us even really trying. We haven't actively gone out and really marketed the country," Summers said.

"Nearly 40 million people are going to take a cruise in the next 12 months. The industry is booming, and it's wildly competitive."

She said there was a need to support investment in Auckland.

"Auckland is pretty much the major turnaround port for the cruise industry," Summers said.

'It's also the economic generator for the rest of the country -- for all of our wonderful regions -- like Gisborne, and as far down as Bluff and Stewart Island.

"There are 26 different cruise destinations, and they're all in various ways dependent on the success of Auckland."

The case for development

Port of Auckland chief executive Roger Gray said the redevelopment plan reflects a shared commitment to ensuring Auckland remains internationally competitive.

"Around the world, the cruise industry is growing quickly, and this plan outlines how we're actively working to capture that demand and boost the Auckland economy," Gray said.

"We've found innovative solutions to biofouling and we're working with Tātaki Auckland Unlimited to promote Auckland and the unique experiences our great city offers to the world."

The plan included a proposal to redevelop Auckland's waterfront to accommodate large cruise ships.

"We believe we're creating Oceania's best cruise destination and that the potential for cruise in Auckland is huge."

The proposed Port of Auckland's Bledisloe North berth and terminal programme includes:

Development ship berth able to accommodate a large ship of about 350m

Improvement to existing berths

Creation of a seamless airport-to-port experience

Deliver a distinctive Māori-led visitor experience of Tāmaki Makaurau.

Improving existing cruise facilities and accessibility.

Stronger collaboration across the cruise sector

Better use of data to measure economic, visitor and community outcomes.

Who pays?

Summers said income generated by the cruise industry and its passengers would ultimately fund the development of the Auckland gateway, rather than the region's ratepayers.

She said tourists paid a $100 international visa, which was used to fund various infrastructure as well as conservation efforts.

"Cruise lines are also paying to come alongside every port that they go into.

"They're paying various taxes every single time they drop an anchor or go alongside in a destination."

She said Auckland was primed for an increase in visitors.

World.title: Binders can be ‘life-changing’ for trans people. But are they safe to exercise in?
World.content:
AFLW player Tilly Lucas-Rodd remembers the "trans joy" they felt the first time they wore a chest binder.

"It was incredible," they said.

"It was so relieving … I remember I put a T-shirt on, and I was like, 'this is life-changing.'"

GWS player Lucas-Rodd is non-binary, and has since had top surgery, a procedure that involves the removal of breast tissue. They have spoken openly to the ABC about how the gender-affirming operation brought their body in line with how they had "always seen [themselves] internally".

Before top surgery, Lucas-Rodd relied on chest binders to reduce gender dysphoria — a psychological term used to describe the distress that can arise when someone experiences a "mismatch" between their gender identity and the sex they were assigned with at birth.

Binding is common among trans men, non-binary and masculine-identifying people who were assigned female at birth.

Tilly Lucas-Rodd wants to share their gender identity journey to help others who can relate. (Getty: Emily Barker)

Anecdotally, however, binding can also have unwanted side-effects, including discomfort, pain, overheating, breathing restrictions, skin irritation and more. Many trans and gender diverse people also believe it may be harmful to bind while exercising, a fear Lucas-Rodd shared.

They experienced skin chafing and "scarring" under their armpits from a string of ill-fitting binders and took to the internet to try and find information on binding while playing sport.

"There wasn't a lot of research," they said.

"But my need and desire to bind kind of outweighed [my fears].

"I was like, I feel so uncomfortable that I'll take some of those negative side effects if they happen."

Australian researchers are now trying to close the gap on a lack of knowledge about binding and exercise, with preliminary results from one study led by the Mental Health and Exercise Research Group at the University of Western Australia (UWA), providing some reassurance.

Loading Instagram content

Largest study yet finds 'comforting' preliminary results

The UWA-led project, done in conjunction with Curtin University, The University of New South Wales, The Kids Research Institute and Thriving in Motion, studied a group of 21 people who were assigned female at birth to see if there were any significant differences between exercising with or without a binder.

No-one in the group had previously worn a chest binder, and all were issued a commercial binder by researchers who had been trained in correct fitting.

Participants took part in two separate exercise sessions — one with and one without a binder — and were put through tests to assess their aerobic fitness, muscle strength and lung function amongst other measures.

Participants in the study were put through tests with and without wearing a binder. (Supplied: UWA)

Researchers found no significant differences when participants were wearing or not wearing a binder, a finding PhD candidate Kai Schweizer says helps dispel the "non-evidence based" perception that binding while exercising is unsafe.

"The findings are really interesting and somewhat comforting," he said.

"We don't have enough evidence to say anything with certainty yet, but our sample was — believe it or not — the largest collected in this area so far.

"Our research is not a definitive answer but it's the first step in trying to better understand the impact of binding on exercise."

As Schweizer explains it, trans and gender diverse people already participate in sport and physical activity at much lower rates than the general population.

PhD candidate Kai Schweizer says the research doesn't give definitive answers, but it's a step closer to understanding the impacts. (Supplied)

"That then contributes to the really high disparities in things like cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes and osteoporosis," Schweizer explains.

"One of the barriers to exercise we identified was the perception among trans folk that it was unsafe to exercise in a chest binder.

"Hopefully this research inspires further, more detailed, bigger studies so that we can try and reduce barriers for trans and gender diverse people to exercise."

One limitation of the UWA study is that they only studied the impacts of binding in the short-term.

However, Schweizer points to a pilot study conducted last year, which followed a group of eighteen trans and gender diverse teenagers, most of whom had been binding for over a year, and found that wearing a binder did not impact exercise capacity.

"We'll need more longitudinal data to really answer the safety question, but I was glad to see that other researchers had started looking at this and their findings didn't substantially differ from ours," he added.

Lucas-Rodd felt 'trans-joy' the first time they wore a binder. (Getty Images: Mark Evans)

The importance of finding the right fit

The findings of the Australian study, which are currently under peer-review, come as welcome news to Adam Brownhill, medical director of a gender-affirming care clinic in Melbourne.

"A healthy lifestyle is an important lifestyle, so anything we find or learn that helps improve inclusion and participation in sport is really, really important," Dr Brownhill said.

"This is a really reassuring piece of research, in that there was no harm found."

Dr Brownhill does, however, emphasise the importance of finding the right type of binder, and correct fit, to ensure safety while exercising.

He says DIY methods like taping can damage the skin if done repeatedly, and cause harm.

"It's like anything — a pair of glasses, a bra, a pair of shoes — you need to make sure it fits properly when you're using it."

Finding the right fit is essential when looking for a binder to exercise in. (Supplied)

There are several custom binding manufacturers in Australia, including Sock Drawer Heroes — who supplied the binders worn in the UWA study — and Transform Transwear, a Melbourne-based company created by Simone Kelly.

Kelly's stepson Eli came out as trans seven years ago but was unable to find any binders available for sale in Australia. Kelly says she was forced to order items from overseas for Eli that were expensive, took a long time to arrive, and were "cheaply made" and "poorly designed".

The experience left her "sad and angry" and fuelled her passion to provide a physical space where trans and gender diverse people could be fitted safely and in private. Since opening their Melbourne-based store in 2024, Transform have serviced clients like Lucas-Rodd, and recently released a binder designed specifically for swimming.

Simone Kelly (right) opened Transform Transwear so that people looking for binders could be fitted properly. (Supplied)

"We get people coming in for swimwear and talking about how long it has been since they've been able to swim," Kelly said.

"Someone came in recently and said, 'I used to love surfing with my Dad as a kid, but I haven't done it in such a long time. So I'm really excited to get out and surf with my Dad.'

"We know young people getting out there and exercising is really fantastic for their mental health, but many are consumed by their dysphoria and don't feel comfortable enough to go and do things like that."

While Kelly acknowledges that the preliminary findings of the UWA study are only the beginning, she says research like it is critical for trans and gender diverse people's health.

"Right up until this research came out, we were telling our customers, don't exercise in a binder and don't sleep in a binder," she said.

"Obviously we need to do more research to help give us more detailed guidance, but this is a great start. It's a step in the right direction."

World.title: The Kiss era has begun, and new coach Les is seeking the 'Wallaby way'
World.content:
The new Wallabies era began with a win in tough conditions against an improving nation, but coach Les Kiss wants more than just wins to be the legacy of his tenure.

The Wallabies head to the Queensland city of Townsville this Saturday for the second and final Test against Japan, after being pushed all the way in Osaka by the Brave Blossoms last weekend.

With the anticipation of Kiss's first match in charge in the rear-view mirror, the former Queensland and Australia rugby league representative is now plotting the Wallabies' bid for success at a home Rugby World Cup late next year.

Wallabies survive scare as Kiss era begins with win New Wallabies coach Les Kiss says his side will need to learn how to control their ambitions after Australia hangs on to win a frantic Test match against Japan in the Osaka heat.

The next step is this Saturday against Japan, the first match between the two nations on Australian soil in 39 years.

But Kiss is seeking more than just Test match victories. He wants the current group of Wallabies to play with a passion that embodies pride, passion and the Australian spirit.

The new Australian boss spoke on ABC Radio Sydney on Wednesday morning, where he outlined what he hoped to foster during his tenure.

"One thing I don’t want to miss in this whole journey is to find a Wallaby way that they are really proud of and blaze their own trail," Kiss said.

"We’ve had some great Wallaby teams in the past; they should be inspiring us and we should empower this group to blaze a trail and make a Wallabies’ way that his their way."

Wallaby fans got a glimpse into the culture Kiss wants to instil when he was captured on the television broadcast having a laugh in the coaching box during the second half of last weekend's three-point win over Japan.

Asked about that moment, Kiss said it was a brief moment where humour was able to ease the tension during a hard-fought Test.

"It shouldn’t all be just a frown … or that your head’s so deep in something that you can’t enjoy the process as well," he told ABC Radio Sydney.

"I think that’s part of the Aussie spirit. We’re competitive, we’ll fight for anything, but we’ll have a crack and a bit of fun along the way.

"This means a lot to me. I know there is a lot at stake for the game here.

"We want to make sure we can do the right thing to continue to grow that game."

Kiss's desire for his players to enjoy the privilege of being a Wallaby appears to be rubbing off.

Angus Bell came off the bench during last week's win over Japan. (Getty Images: Paul Miller)

Prop Angus Bell, a second-generation Wallaby, told media on Wednesday that Kiss has focused on ensuring each player embraces each opportunity to represent Australia.

"Week to week, you get sort of caught in the washing machine of what Test match rugby is. You're always bashing each other, trying to get better at training and you get lost in how special a Test match is," Bell said.

"Test matches don't come around often; people don't get many caps.

"So I think what Les touches on is how special it is if you get the opportunity in the [team], how awesome it is, because one day it all stops.

"He's really just instilled in us how actually special it is to represent the Wallabies."

On the field, Kiss has some decisions to make about who plays in Townsville on Saturday afternoon.

Lock Miles Amatosero was handed a three-match suspension after being red-carded for head contact in a breakdown, opening up a starting spot in the middle row.

Joseph-Aukuso Sua'ali'i was ruled out earlier this week after suffering hamstring soreness, with Italy-bound Josh Flook coming into the squad.

Queensland Reds prop Massimo De Lutiis has also been brought into the squad, and could be in line to make his international debut if selected on Thursday. Should De Lutiis be picked and play on Saturday, he would become the 1,000th Wallaby.

Following last week's win over Japan, and a 57-10 triumph over Italy last month, the Wallabies are attempting to win three Tests in a row for the first time in two years.

ABC Sport will have live blog coverage of the second Test between the Wallabies and Japan on Saturday afternoon from 2pm AEST.

World.title: Ex-Wallabies, league star Brian Smith dies of cancer
World.content:
Wallabies prop Angus Bell is leading the tributes for dual rugby union international and former NRL star Brian Smith, who has died aged 59.

Smith, who played six Tests for Australia in 1987 and nine for Ireland after switching allegiance, had battled cancer.

Once described by former Wallabies coach Alan Jones as one of the world's most gifted players, Smith was most recently the Head of Sport at Scots College in Sydney, where Bell and many other Wallabies graduated from.

"He was coaching at the Scots school and coached a lot of us coming through the grades and I just wanted to say it's a really sad time," Bell said from Wallabies camp in Townsville on Wednesday.

"We're wishing the best for his wife and kids. He's an avid rugby person and helped a lot of individuals in the squad and in the Wallabies today, so just sending my condolences from both the Wallabies and myself."

Australia's 999th Wallaby's Test debut Isaac Henry will run the prospect of fresh ink past his wife but is otherwise assured he can make a permanent Wallabies mark after a hard-earned debut in Osaka.

Smith, who also played 43 games for Balmain and Eastern Suburbs from 1991 to 1994, coached Bell at GPS and NSW schoolboys' level when the emerging front-rower was only 16.

"Fair to say that I wouldn't have played as good or anywhere near as good without him," Bell said.

"Me, Jeremy Williams and Will Harris from the (Western) Force were really close with him and he was a great bloke, a great father and a great coach.

"So, yeah, very sad."

After playing schoolboys' rugby for Australia, Smith made his Wallabies debut under Jones in 1987, partnering Nick Farr-Jones in the halves and bagging 18 points from a try, five conversions and a penalty in a 65-18 win over South Korea.

Australian forward Angus Bell - in Wallabies camp in Townsville - paid tribute to his former high school coach and mentor Brian Smith. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

After his playing career, Smith coached in Japan and England, where he was the national team's attack coach, and served as Australia's sevens coach.

"Brian had been very unwell in recent months and was battling an aggressive cancer," Scots College principal Dr Ian PM Lambert wrote to school colleagues.

"This is very sad news for our College community and I know it will come as a shock to many of you who knew and worked closely with him.

"Our immediate thoughts are with Brian's wife Lisa, his daughters Ruby and Santana, and his son Chilli."

AAP

World.title: Former Hurricanes cricketer jailed for abusing 15yo girl
World.content:
A former Hobart Hurricanes cricket player will serve 10 months in prison for sexually abusing a child.

WARNING: This story contains details of child sexual abuse.

Aaron William Summers, 30, pleaded guilty to two counts of penetrative sexual abuse of a young person and one count of grooming in June in the Supreme Court of Tasmania, after having previously pleaded not guilty.

In court on Wednesday, he was sentenced to two-and-a-half years in jail, suspended after 10 months, meaning he will leave prison in April next year.

Justice Helen Wood told the court that Summers met the victim at a Hobart Hurricanes cricket match in 2017.

The following month, the 15-year-old girl attended another game and spoke to Summers, who was 21 at the time.

Aaron Summers was playing for the Hobart Hurricanes when he met the 15-year-old girl. (Getty Images: Robert Prezioso)

The pair began messaging on social media, and Summers arranged to pick her up from her home later that night.

The court heard he drove her to a local primary school, laid down a blanket, and sexually abused her twice.

Justice Wood told the court that Summers knew she was under the age of 17 and at high school, but did not ask how old she was.

"She thought they were meeting to talk; in reality, she represented a sexual opportunity to him," Justice Wood said.

"She was vulnerable because of her age and innocence; he had said nothing to warn her of his real motives."

The grooming charge related to social media conversations between Summers and the girl, in which Summers sent explicit photos of himself and requested photos from her.

"As a community, we look up to sportspeople; young people are likely to admire them, see them in a positive light," Justice Woods said.

"His role as a sportsperson gave him contact with young people, and enabled the commission of his crimes; this is an aggravating factor."

In November 2021, Summers pleaded guilty to charges in the Northern Territory, including possessing and transmitting child abuse material and transmitting communication with someone under 16 with the intention of procuring the recipient to engage in, or make, sexual activity.

Summers served three years and 11 months in prison in the NT. He was arrested on the day of his release and extradited to Tasmania to face these charges.

Cricket career 'at an end'

Justice Wood said Summers had experienced social isolation, loneliness and depressive symptoms while playing cricket in Tasmania and was spending excessive time on social media.

She said once he moved to the Northern Territory, he had established a successful career playing cricket in Australia and overseas and had a high profile.

"Due to the crimes, his future as a professional cricketer is at an end," she said.

Twenty months of the sentence was suspended, meaning Aaron Summers (left) is set for release in April next year. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Justice Wood said that Summers has accepted responsibility for his crimes and understood the impact his offending has had on his victims.

In the NT, he completed an intensive sex offender treatment program, which involved over 100 sessions, in which Justice Wood told the court he engaged appropriately and gained insight into his offending.

Justice Wood said when deciding on his sentence, she considered the lengthy jail time he had already served in the NT after the Tasmanian crimes were committed, and the significant progress he has taken towards his rehabilitation.

"[The] understanding he has about the harm he has caused and he is motivated to regain his life," she said.

Justice Wood imposed a sentence of two-and-a-half years, backdated to June 28 of this year, due to the time he has spent in remand.

She suspended the last 20 months of the sentence, with strict conditions, such as obliging him to comply with his probation officers and submit to psychological treatment.

The court heard that Summers would likely return to Western Australia, where he is from and his family live, to serve out his suspended sentence once he is able to leave prison in April next year.

World.title: 'Can't compete': Super coaches weigh into PNG Chiefs debate
World.content:
Trent Robinson won't be raging about the inequality of the tax breaks afforded to the PNG Chiefs, even if he believes the NRL's open market is no longer a "level playing field".

After Penrith winger Brian To'o became the sixth player wooed by the start-up franchise's tax-free wages, Panthers coach Ivan Cleary declared clubs "can't compete" with the bounty the Chiefs can provide from 2028.

Cleary revealed he was in tears when To'o informed him he would leave Penrith to join the Chiefs, who critics — led by South Sydney coach Wayne Bennett — have said now have an unfair advantage in attracting talent.

The salary cap has been an equaliser of talent but Bennett has claimed the NRL has eroded the competition's fairness by giving the Chiefs such an upper hand.

The Chiefs' advantages are in contrast to the few concessions afforded to the Perth Bears, who will enter the NRL next season.

Chiefs sign premiership winger To'o away from Panthers Four-time premiership-winning winger Brian To'o has become the sixth player to sign with the PNG Chiefs for their inaugural NRL season in 2028.

"It's not a level playing field and I think you can see that," said Sydney Roosters coach Robinson.

"We've got (it on) one (hand) where we feel like it's not a level playing field and the other where we feel like they need more assistance.

"We're going to debate … but do we want our game to grow?

"We're not going to stop at 19 (teams) … we should own the Pacific.

"If we want more money in the game, want to expand, we need more teams, so I think it's a positive thing — players are going to go."

Penrith were the latest club to feel that pinch when they gave To'o, who enters the last 12 months of his deal in November, a seven-day window to explore his options for 2028.

Premiership-winning Panthers Jarome Luai and Brian To'o will reunite in 2028 at the Chiefs. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The winger signed with the Chiefs without visiting PNG, joining Jarome Luai, Connor Watson, Alex Johnston and Zac Lomax in agreeing to deals with the NRL's 19th side.

Loading Instagram content

"I had a little moment the other day, just very sad that Bizza's going to be going," the usually stoic Cleary said.

"There would've been a few (tears) … It's just hard to imagine 'Biz' playing in any other jersey. But there's a few guys out there that I thought the same."

Since their rise to premiership dominance in 2020, the Panthers have become accustomed to salary cap pressure squeezing out key players.

But they are especially vulnerable after 2027, with the cashed-up Chiefs emerging just as they battle to hold on to co-captains Isaah Yeo and Nathan Cleary, as well as premiership players Paul Alamoti, Liam Martin and Moses Leota.

"I think everyone knows with the Chiefs, it's hard to match that stuff," Cleary said.

"It's not your average club, but if players want to go there, you can't compete."

Asked whether the Chiefs had unfairly skewed the player market, Cleary recalled some wisdom from Marty Gurr, who was on the coaching staff during his early playing days at Manly.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I remember when I first played 35 years ago, my first coach said to me 'rugby league isn't fair'," Cleary said.

"I think he was right. I've worked that out along the way. Whether it's fair or not, that's what the game's gone with. I can understand it."

Since overcoming the initial emotional blow of To'o's impending exit, Cleary has turned his attention to Penrith's task of retaining their stable of stars before September.

"We're very hopeful of having a few of them done (soon), you definitely don't want to be going into the finals doing this sort of stuff," he said.

AAP

World.title: Legendary boot-studder hangs up his own after 58 years with Port Adelaide
World.content:
He's outlasted big names and seen many more games without the limelight but after nearly six decades looking after boots for Port Adelaide Football Club, Alfie Trebilcock is hanging up his own.

A young butcher from Broken Hill who came to the club during 1968, the boot-studder enjoyed 11 SANFL premierships, one AFL premiership, and watched footwear evolve from ankle-high boots with wooden knock-in sprigs, to light-weight multi-coloured fashion statements.

"I came down here [to Adelaide] in 1961. My grandparents followed Port Adelaide so I started following them and used to go to their games and all that type of thing," Trebilcock told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"I got friendly with the runner, Harry Vincent, got talking one day and said I'd like to get into the club and he said, 'I'll keep an eye out for you'."

A position opened up in the boot department and Trebilcock was told to have a "talk to the sprigger" who was also a bootmaker.

"He said, 'Are you prepared to learn?', and I said, 'Oh yeah', so I did a seven-year apprenticeship with him," Trebilcock said.

"After those seven years he got leukaemia and said, 'You're going to have to take over', and I said, 'Gee whiz, I'm a butcher'.

" But I was pretty lucky because moulded soles were coming in then and so I took it on and I've been there ever since and enjoyed every single minute of it. "

But from the day Trebilcock started looking after the players' footwear in 1968 and up to 1976, the Port Adelaide Magpies played without winning a SANFL premiership.

"I was beginning to think I was jinx," Trebilcock said.

But the club won a flag in 1977 and another 10 during Trebilcock's time, as well as a 2004 AFL premiership with its AFL side, The Power.

"The 2004 AFL premiership was mighty.

"I always pictured standing on the MCG on Grand Final day, celebrating a flag. That dream came true in 2004. I'll never, ever forget that day."

Bobby to say farewell as well

Also retiring is fellow volunteer Bob "Bobby" O'Malley after 18 years at the club mixing water barrels and player rehydration bottles, and helping set up for training sessions.

Former Port Adelaide Power player and captain Travis Boak with Bob O'Malley during a game against Carlton. (Supplied: Port Adelaide Football Club)

"I just loved being involved in this football club," he said.

"Port Adelaide was always a family club, and all my family barracked for Port Adelaide."

He will have his final home game with Port Adelaide against Melbourne on Saturday night.

Trebilcock will be saying goodbye after 58 years with the club.

He said he became "real friends" during this time with the late and great Russel Ebert OAM, who started with the Magpies the same year as him.

An Australian Football Hall of Fame member since 1996, Ebert played 392 games for the Magpies and remains the only SANFL player to win four Magarey Medals.

"He was a people's person," Trebilcock said.

"He was a player that never played a game of football in moulded sole boots. To the day he retired he still had knock-in sprigs.

"Every now and then you'd have to re-sprig his boots.

"As he got older his sprigging would change … then he got his Achilles problems and we made a [raised] heel for him."

The late Russell Ebert shares a laugh with Alfie Trebilcock at Port Adelaide Football Club. (Supplied: Port Adelaide Football Club)

Ebert once said of Trebilcock that he loved the players and the club, and the players loved him.

"He can talk to any player at any time and would have the complete respect of the entire playing and coaching group … we couldn't have had the success we had without him," Ebert said.

The AFL awarded Trebilcock the Jack Titus Award for conspicuous service to the game in 2013.

He was awarded Life Membership at PAFC in 2013 and was inducted into its Hall of Fame in 2025.

PAFC chairman David Koch said the club was what it was today because of people like O'Malley and Trebilcock.

"Nearly 60 years of turning up, asking for nothing and giving everything to the club he loves," he said.

"On behalf of every player, coach and supporter we say thank you, Alfie, and thank you, Bobby. We are the club we are today because of people like you."

World.title: 'Nowhere to hide' for Australia's under-fire batters against Bangladesh
World.content:
Former Australian Test opener Ed Cowan says some of Australia's batters are under pressure to make significant scores as the summer of cricket begins against Bangladesh in the Top End this week.

"If you're in the Australian Test team, and not performing regularly, there is just nowhere to hide," Cowan said on the ABC Cricket Podcast.

"And unfortunately, sometimes you get these weaker teams, and the expectation actually goes up. Cricket is hard enough, let alone with the weight of the world on your shoulders."

The Australian team is about to enter a 12-month period with potentially 21 Tests scheduled, including key away fixtures in India, South Africa and England.

Between June 2025 and the start of this cycle tomorrow, they played eight Tests, five of which were in Australia.

Australia played five of their eight Tests over the last 12 months at home, including the Ashes against England. (AAP: Dave Hunt)

"That's two careers, 21 Test matches. You could have two careers in that time. That's a lot of Test cricket," Cowan said.

That cycle begins in Darwin when they take on Bangladesh, a nation ranked ninth in the ICC Test rankings.

At the conclusion of the recent successful Ashes series against England, the average age of the Australian team was just under 34. This is a team that has played together and had great success for a long time.

The Test between Australia and Bangladesh starts on Thursday August 13 in Darwin, and you can hear every ball live on ABC Listen.

Cowan does not believe that playing lower-ranked opposition necessarily provides younger players with a chance to gain experience.

"I think you are trying to pick your best available team and there's always an opportunity to work through your portfolio of players, and they've done this in recent years, usually away from home and it's less opposition dependent and more condition dependent," he said.

The bowling attack has been well established for some time with the likes of Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood, Pat Cummins and Nathan Lyon proving a recipe for success.

Where the questions creep in is around the batting line-up.

Jake Weatherald was given an opportunity to open the batting in the recent Ashes series but is yet to score an international century, with a top score of 72.

Jake Weatherald will be looking to impress in front of his home crowd in Darwin against Bangladesh (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Cowan expects the Northern Territory product to open in the first game, but says he remains under pressure.

"If Jake Weatherald doesn't get 100 in the next five Test matches, more than likely we'll find someone who will get an opportunity to open the batting. And so there's going to be some natural attrition over the coming months," he said.

He is not the only player who will be searching for form in this two-match series against Bangladesh. Marnus Labuschagne has averaged 26.61 with the bat in his last 20 tests and has taken time away from playing to focus on a training block in Queensland.

"After eight weeks of being able to just go back to my fundamentals and working on my game, spending hours and hours on the simple things, just my shots, working on my shapes and my technique as a whole, is something that I definitely needed," Labuschagne told reporters in Brisbane last week.

Loading Instagram content

It has been over 1,100 days since he last reached triple figures in a Test match back in 2023. Cowan believes these Tests could be a step in the right direction for Labuschagne.

"The greatest thing that you can have as a Test batsman is confidence. And confidence is only bred through performance," he said.

The youngest member of Australia's most recent Test team is Cameron Green. When the West Australian debuted in 2020, aged 21, he was touted as one of the best young talents in the country, but his recent form has some questioning his future in the side.

The now 27-year-old has played 37 Tests and has a batting average of 32.75 and a bowling average of 38.94, but Australian coach Andrew McDonald is resolute that Green remains a vital member of his side.

"We believe Cam Green is a very, very skilled player, and we believe, sometimes, his performances have been taken a little bit out of context," McDonald told SEN Radio.

"He's been contributing to this team, as have a lot of that top seven, in conditions that haven't been favourable to batters."

Cowan believes these two Tests present an opportunity for those out of form to find some form at a time when there is less pressure coming from other domestic players.

The last time Australia played a Test against Bangladesh was 2017, where Australia won the series 2-1. (Getty Images: /SOPA Images/LightRocket/Md Manik)

"They get first crack at it. And when there's no other cricket going on, there was a CA XI game that we'll come to, but there's no Shield cricket, there's no Aussie A tours, no-one's putting pressure on anyone," he said.

"It's a bit of a free swing. And in many respects, that should free the batters up to just go and play."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: High school American footballer rattled by snake in helmet
World.content:
A high school American football player in the United States had every right to be rattled after finding a venomous snake inside his helmet during practice.

A team was going through its paces at Maumelle High school in Central Arkansas when a student felt unusual movement inside his headgear following warm-ups and brought his helmet to an assistant coach for inspection.

A slithering 2-foot (61cm) cottonmouth was discovered behind some padding.

The pit viper was so reluctant to exit the helmet that police officers had to pour water into it to force the snake out and into a bag.

Animal services technicians arrived a few minutes later, identified the snake as a deadly cottonmouth and took it to a wooded area far from the school.

Cottonmouths are the second-most-venomous snakes found in Arkansas.

Snake caught in bike chain bites woman The woman, in her 60s, was riding on a northern NSW rail trail when she ran over a two-metre snake that became trapped then bit her.

Animal services director Chris Davis said the player wore the helmet for nearly an hour and was fortunate he was not bitten.

"It was unreal," Davis said. "You had to kind of be there and take pictures to say this was real."

The player grabbed a different helmet and continued practice.

But the situation caused the head coach to reiterate to his team that players should examine their equipment carefully before using it, to check for insects or anything larger and more dangerous.

AP

Tech.title: The next big indie game publisher is taking some exciting swings
Tech.content:
Players take on the role of Diana, a woman who discovers she can receive visions of the future after an experimental implant is embedded into her brain.

Players will be tasked with exploring these visions of the future, focusing on specific moments and committing them to Diana’s memory in the present day. Prescience comes with consequences, however, and as soon as Diana commits a detail to memory, the very future ahead of her changes.

Tech.title: It looks like Apple’s iPhone 18 really will skip the fall launch this year
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

According to an Economic Daily News report spotted by MacRumors, executives for Apple supplier Pegatron confirmed during an earnings call that the iPhone 18 Pro series phones will launch this fall, but the base iPhone 18 won’t arrive until the first quarter of next year. The more affordable iPhone 18e and a new iPhone Air are also rumored to launch around the same time, in line with rumors that have been circulating for more than a year.

Analyst Ming-Chi Kuo and The Information both reported last year that Apple was planning to only launch its premium iPhones in fall 2026, and earlier this year another Apple supplier said one of its customers was postponing a phone launch to early 2027.

Along with the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple’s rumored “Ultra” foldable is reportedly launching this fall. The EDN report cites Pegatron execs saying that memory and chip shortages are causing the peak shipping seasons to shift, as its customers like Apple figure out how to spread out the parts they have and increasingly prioritize higher-priced models that have larger margins.

Tech.title: Google’s Pixel 11 phone preorders come with up to $350 in gift cards
Tech.content:
Brad Bourque is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Looking to get your hands on the latest Pixel devices? After weeks of leaks and rumors, Google has officially announced its next generation of Pixel phones and watches.

The base Pixel 11 starts at $899, the Pro and Pro XL are $1,099 and $1,299 respectively, and the Pro Fold starts at $1,899. The watch comes in two sizes, with the smaller 41mm model starting at $399, and the larger 45mm model starting at $429. The phones are available for preorder now, and will ship on August 20th, 2026.

If you’re looking to preorder an unlocked phone on its own, your main options are Best Buy, Amazon, and directly from the Google Store. All three are running a similar introductory deal, where you’ll receive a gift card for a future purchase at that retailer, with the value depending on which model you buy. The Pixel 11 includes a $100 gift card, the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL include a $200 gift card, and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold includes a $350 gift card. Only Google lists an end date for the promotion, which is August 27th, 2026.

If you’d also like a Pixel Watch 5, Google is the best option, because you can opt to put the gift card towards the purchase of the Watch instead to earn an extra $50 on top of the value. For example, if you buy a Pixel 11 Pro, you can take a $200 gift card, or opt for $250 off the Pixel Watch 5 when purchased together. If you buy a Pixel 11 Pro Fold, the base model 41mm Pixel Watch 5 is free.

Each phone is powered by the new Tensor G6 processor, which Google says is capable of 25 percent faster web browsing and 15 percent improvement to app loading speeds over the Tensor G5. The camera and video features are a focus of the new Pixel 11 series phones. The new Magic Capture feature lets you forget about snapping a great shot, and instead stitches together a series of clips and photos from a longer video. All four phones also featuring upgraded batteries and fast charging, with wireless charging support for Qi2.2 up to 25W.

If you’re deciding which Pixel is right for you, make sure to check out our initial hands-on impressions for the new Pixel 11 series phones and the Pixel Watch 5.

Where to preorder the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL

The Pixel 11 Pro starts at $1,099 for the base model with 256GB of storage, and goes up to $1,219 for the 512GB model, or $1,449 for the 1TB model. The larger Pixel 11 Pro XL starts at $1,299 for the 256GB configuration, with the 512GB costing $1,419 and the 1TB model priced at $1,649. For both phones, the 256GB version has 12GB of memory, while the larger capacity models have 16GB of memory.

Apart from the screen size, resolution, and battery capacity, the two phones are otherwise identical to each other. They feature updated cameras, including a 50MP wide angle, 48MP telephoto with up to 5x optical zoom, a 48MP ultrawide sensor, and a 42MP selfie camera with a 103 degree field of view. The phones are available in four colors: canyon, fog, olive, and obsidian.

Where to preorder the Pixel 11

The Pixel 11 starts at $899 for the model with 256GB of storage, and the price rising to $1,019 for the 512GB model, both of which have 12GB of memory. The 6.3-inch display has a 1080 x 2424 resolution and 60-120Hz refresh rate, with HDR support up to 2000 nits, or 3000 nit brightness with HDR off. For cameras, the Pixel 11 sports a 48MP sensor wide camera, a 13MP ultrawide, a 10.8 MP telephoto with 5x optical zoom, and a 10.5MP selfie camera with a 95 degree field of view. The phone is available in four colors: frost, pistachio, hibiscus, and obsidian.

Where to preorder the Pixel 11 Pro Fold

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold starts at $1,899 for the base model with 256GB and 16GB of RAM, with a 512GB model for $2,019, and a 1TB option for $2,249 available as well. It’s available in two colors: olive and obsidian.

The only foldable phone in Google’s Pixel lineup, the 11 Pro Fold features a 6.5-inch external display, and a 8-inch internal display when opened. Both screens feature refresh rates up to 120Hz, and HDR support. The internal and front selfie cameras are 10MP sensors, and the main camera block features a 10.5MP ultrawide, 10.8MP telephoto with up to 5X optical zoom, and a new 48MP wide camera with upgraded light sensitivity.

Where to preorder the Pixel Watch 5

The updated Pixel Watch 5 comes in two sizes, with the 41mm model starting at $399, and the larger 45mm model starting at $429. In addition to faster processing and more memory, there are a variety of new features for exercising, like a workout builder, and a more accurate GPS in crowded areas. The watch adds a variety of new long-term health features under the umbrella of “Health Guardian” which can detect some medical emergencies, watch blood pressure trends, and keep track of insulin resistance.

Carrier offers and promotions

AT&T is offering a variety of discounts if you want to upgrade to the new phones or the Pixel Watch 5. Most notably, you can get a Pixel 11 Pro for free via 36 months of credits if you trade in a Pixel phone of any year or condition, although you’ll need to keep the service active for the duration and have a service of at least $80 a month. The same deal is available for a Pixel 11 Pro XL with qualified trade-ins. If you’re starting a new line and buying a device that’s $500 or more with an installment plan, you can also claim 50 percent off a Pixel Watch 5.

Tech.title: Twitch streamers can now opt out from training Amazon’s AI
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Twitch users can now opt out of allowing their content to be used to train Amazon’s generative AI models. Opting out means that “your streams, VODs, clips, stream chats, and pictures and text on your channel” won’t be used in “future training” of an Amazon AI model “whose purpose is to generate or synthesize text, audio, images, or video,” according to a Twitch support page.

Other “AI-supported” features like captions and safety tools will still function if you opt-out of generative AI training. However, if you participate in a chat on another person’s stream, “their opt-out preferences govern if that chat can be used for training,” Twitch says.

The “Training for Generative AI” toggle is present for me in Twitch’s settings under the Security and Privacy tab. It was toggled on when I found it, and I’ve asked Amazon if that’s the default.

Here’s the full text of Amazon’s description for the toggle:

Allow your channel content to train generative AI content models at Amazon. Turning this off does not opt you out of Twitch and Amazon using your channel content for other purposes described in the Twitch Privacy Notice, including using AI-supported Twitch features that benefit the community by facilitating streamer growth and monetization (such as real-time sponsorship campaign assistance), viewer discovery (such as recommendations), and community safety (such as AutoMod). Learn more

Tech.title: How Google’s new Pixel 11 phones compare to last year’s models
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google just added four new phones to the Pixel family: the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. They’re slightly more expensive than their predecessors, but they come with some notable upgrades, including improved cameras and a new Tensor G6 chip that should deliver faster performance. The phones also have new photography tools, like Magic Capture, along with improvements to Gemini Intelligence, expanded Live Translate capabilities, and the ability to use Circle to Search directly through the camera.

To make deciding whether you’ll upgrade or hold onto your last-gen phone a little simpler, we’re focusing on comparing the specs of the 6.3-inch Pixel 11 and Pixel 10 models, as well as the 6.8-inch Pro XL models. If you’re curious about how the Pixel 11 Pro Fold compares to its predecessor (and to the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 series foldables), we’ve got a spec comparison right here.

Before we get to the specs, here’s a breakdown of what’s new.

They’re more expensive, but you get more storage

The most obvious difference is that, like almost everything these days, they’re more expensive than before. The Pixel 11 starts at $899, $100 more than its predecessor, but Google has doubled the base storage to 256GB with 12GB of RAM. The Pixel 11 Pro starts at $1,099 — $100 more than the Pixel 10 Pro’s launch price — with the same 256GB of storage and 12GB of RAM, and is available with up to 1TB of storage and 16GB of RAM. Meanwhile, Google’s larger 6.8-inch Pixel 11 Pro XL starts at $1,299 and offers the same storage and RAM configurations as the Pro.

Tensor G6 allows for even more AI features

Both the Pixel 11 and Pro phones run on Google’s new Tensor G6 chip, which the company claims should improve performance by up to 25 percent compared to its predecessor. The new chip also powers a host of AI upgrades, including improvements to Gemini Intelligence, which Google says can now pull more context from supported apps to proactively surface useful information. There are also new voice-to-text tools that remove filler words and clean up formatting, while writing assistance can use what’s on your screen to help draft, rewrite, and refine messages. Live Translate is also available on videos, podcasts, and voice messages, and Circle to Search now works directly through the camera, letting you identify objects, translate text, or search your surroundings without snapping a photo first.

The cameras get some notable upgrades inside and out

There are a number of camera improvements, too, along with new photography and video features. On the hardware side, the Pixel 11 has a slimmer camera bar that sits flush when paired with one of Google’s phone cases. It can also zoom in farther than its predecessor, reaching up to 30x for photos, while the Pixel 11 Pro series gets an updated 1/1.3-inch 50-megapixel sensor for its main camera and a redesigned telephoto sensor that Google says captures 32 percent more light. The Pro can also zoom up to 120x and features a 42-megapixel selfie camera. The Pro should be quicker at shooting in the dark, too, with Google claiming its Instant Night Sight can capture photos up to 4.5 times faster.

Google has made several software improvements as well. The new Magic Capture mode in the camera app automatically captures photos and videos to make them ready to share with a tap. Camera Looks let you create custom styles for photos, while the Pixel 11 Pro series can record stabilized video at up to 8K using Pro Stable Video with Video Boost. A new Creator Suite also features tools for trimming and rearranging clips, using a teleprompter while recording, and improving speech clarity, and it automatically saves clips to a designated project album.

How the Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 compare

Those are some of the biggest changes, but they’re far from the only differences between the two lineups. For example, both the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro offer an Extreme Charging Mode that prioritizes charging over other tasks for a faster boost when you’re short on time. The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL also gets HiLight, colored LEDs around the camera flash that can alert you to things, like calls when your phone is face down or when Gemini is activated.

For a closer look at those changes and everything else that separates the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro from their predecessors, we’ve broken down the specs side by side below.
